blocks.p: This is an Indian examination, so the operative statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963. It is closely modelled on the English Marine Insurance Act 1906 and much of the wording is common, but the 1963 Act is the one to cite. England reformed its own law by the Insurance Act 2015; that reform is English, it did not amend the Indian Act, and it does not govern here.
Section 19: a contract of marine insurance is a contract based upon the utmost good faith, and if utmost good faith be not observed by either party, the contract may be avoided by the other party.

Three features give the principle its shape. The duty is mutual - section 19 says either party, so it binds the underwriter as well as the assured. It operates at the pre-contractual stage, because the underwriter must price a risk whose facts lie almost entirely with the proposer: the ship, her history, her trade and her management are known to the owner and not to the insurer. And it displaces the ordinary commercial rule of caveat emptor - in a marine policy silence about a material fact is itself a breach, whereas in an ordinary contract it usually is not.

Section 20(1): before the contract is concluded the assured must disclose to the insurer every material circumstance which is known to the assured, and the assured is deemed to know every circumstance which in the ordinary course of business ought to be known to him. He cannot escape by not asking his own managers.

Section 20(2) supplies the test. A circumstance is material if it would influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium, or in determining whether he will take the risk. Section 20(4) adds that materiality is in each case a question of fact, and section 20(5) that "circumstance" includes any communication made to, or information received by, the assured.

The duty is not confined to the assured personally. Section 21 imposes the same duty on an agent effecting the insurance, covering what the agent knows and what he ought to know; section 22 requires every material representation made during negotiation to be true.

In underwriting practice the circumstances disclosed typically include: the vessel's age, type, flag, class and standing with her society; ownership and technical management; the intended voyage, trading limits and any war-risk or sanctioned area; the nature, packing and stowage of the cargo; the loss and claims record; and known defects or outstanding conditions of class. (Practice, not statute - the Act states the test, not a list.)

blocks.h: 4. Circumstances which need NOT be disclosed

blocks.p: Section 20(3) gives a closed list of four, and all four are subject to the opening words "in the absence of enquiry":

ol: any circumstance which is known or presumed to be known to the insurer - the insurer is presumed to know matters of common notoriety and matters which an insurer in the ordinary course of his business ought to know;
any circumstance as to which information is waived by the insurer;
any circumstance which it is superfluous to disclose by reason of any express or implied warranty.

blocks.p: The qualifier is doing real work. Once the insurer asks, the exception falls away and the question must be answered truthfully; and section 22 then makes an untrue answer a misrepresentation in its own right.

blocks.h: 5. Effect of non-disclosure at the conclusion of the contract

blocks.p: Section 20(1) states the consequence directly: if the assured fails to make such disclosure, the insurer may avoid the contract.

Avoidance operates ab initio. The contract is treated as never having existed, the premium is normally returnable, and no claim is payable - including a claim wholly unconnected with the matter concealed. Four qualifications complete the answer. It is a right to avoid, not automatic nullity: the policy is voidable, not void, and the insurer may elect to affirm it. That right may be lost by waiver or by delay once the insurer knows the facts. The non-disclosure need not be fraudulent - innocent or negligent concealment of a material circumstance is enough. And because section 19 is mutual, the assured may equally avoid for want of good faith by the insurer.

The question prints as one block of 16 marks but contains four distinct tasks, and the examiner will be marking four things: the principle, what must be disclosed, what need not be, and the consequence. Give each its own heading and the marks are visibly separated on the page. A candidate who writes one long essay on good faith is answering a quarter of the question at length.

The third limb is the cheapest scoring in the question and the one most often skipped. It is a closed statutory list of four items. Written out with the words "in the absence of enquiry" in front of them, it takes ninety seconds and banks the marks. Do it early, before the clock becomes a problem.

blocks.h: The jurisdiction trap - this is the point of the question

blocks.p: Almost every readily available account of uberrimae fidei is written about English law. This examination is Indian. The operative statute is the Marine Insurance Act, 1963: section 19 (utmost good faith), section 20 (disclosure by the assured), section 21 (disclosure by an agent), section 22 (representations). Citing the UK Marine Insurance Act 1906 as the governing statute in an Indian paper is a real and entirely avoidable error, and it is visible to the examiner in one line.

Naming the 1906 Act as the model for the 1963 Act is correct and shows reading. Naming it as the governing law is wrong. The distinction is worth getting right in one clean sentence at the top of the answer.

blocks.h: The English reform, and why it does not belong in the answer

blocks.p: English law on this subject was materially reformed by the Insurance Act 2015, which replaced the blunt all-or-nothing remedy of avoidance with a duty of fair presentation and a scheme of proportionate remedies - so that an innocent non-disclosure which would merely have raised the premium now leads to a proportionate reduction in the claim rather than the loss of cover altogether.

That reform is English and statutory. It did not amend the Indian Act, under which avoidance remains the remedy. Knowing the contrast is worth a sentence and is excellent oral material; writing the English position as though it were the Indian one would be marked wrong.

ul: Citing the Marine Insurance Act 1906 as the governing statute in an Indian examination.
Importing the UK Insurance Act 2015 proportionate remedies into Indian law.
Saying the duty binds only the assured. Section 19 is expressly mutual - either party.
Saying the contract is void. It is voidable at the option of the innocent party.
Omitting the words "in the absence of enquiry" from the section 20(3) exceptions. Once asked, every one of them must be answered.
Claiming the non-disclosure must be fraudulent. It need not be.
Spending the whole answer on the meaning of good faith and never reaching the fourth limb.

"The owner did not mention a grounding two years ago, but it was widely reported in the trade press. Must he disclose it?" Arguably not - section 20(3)(b) excepts circumstances known or presumed known to the insurer, including matters of common notoriety. But if the insurer asks, it must be answered truthfully.

"The undisclosed fact had nothing to do with the loss. Can the insurer still avoid?" Under the Indian Act, yes. Avoidance is not limited to matters causative of the loss. That harshness is precisely what the English 2015 Act was passed to soften - and it has not been softened in India.
"Is the policy void or voidable?" Voidable. The distinction carries a mark on its own, and it is the reason the insurer can affirm.
"The assured disclosed something that made the risk look better. Was he obliged to?" No - section 20(3)(a) excepts circumstances which diminish the risk. Volunteering them is permitted, not required.
"The broker knew but the owner did not." Section 21. The agent effecting the insurance owes the duty for what he knows and what he ought to know.
Which Act governs marine insurance in India, and from what year? The Marine Insurance Act, 1963.
State the test of materiality. Whether the circumstance would influence the judgment of a prudent insurer in fixing the premium or determining whether to take the risk.
List the four circumstances which need not be disclosed.
Is the contract void or voidable? Voidable, at the option of the other party.
Does the duty bind the insurer too? Yes - section 19 says either party.
Can the insurer lose the right to avoid? Yes, by affirming the contract, or by waiver or delay once he knows the facts.

blocks.p: For the four exceptions at section 20(3), use D-K-W-S: Diminishes the risk, Known to the insurer, Waived by the insurer, Superfluous by reason of warranty. Then remember the single gate that sits in front of all four: in the absence of enquiry.

For the sections, the numbers run in the order the answer does: 19 the principle, 20 the duty and its exceptions, 21 the agent, 22 representations. Nineteen through twenty-two, in the order you write them.

questions.understand_first: An underwriter cannot inspect what he is insuring. He is quoting on a ship he has never seen, in a trade he is told about, with a history that only the owner holds. So the law does something it does not do for ordinary contracts: it makes silence a breach. The assured must volunteer everything a careful underwriter would want to know, before the contract is made, and if he does not, the insurer can unwind the policy from the beginning - even if the thing hidden had nothing whatever to do with the eventual claim. Everything in this question follows from that one asymmetry of knowledge. The four limbs are simply: why the rule exists, what it demands, where it stops, and what happens when it is broken.

retrieval_cards.why: The words "either party" are what make the duty mutual, and they are frequently dropped.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must the assured disclose, and what is the test of materiality?

blocks.h: 1. What the Convention is, and the problem it was written to solve

blocks.p: The Convention on Facilitation of International Maritime Traffic, 1965 was adopted on 9 April 1965 and entered into force on 5 March 1967. It is the IMO's facilitation instrument, and it sits apart from SOLAS and MARPOL in what it regulates: not the ship, but the paperwork and formalities imposed on the ship by the shore.

The problem it addressed was over-regulation by accumulation. Every State had developed its own customs, immigration, health and port declarations, so a ship on a multi-port voyage faced a different set of forms in every country, in different formats, demanding the same facts in different ways. The cost was not compliance but delay.

The Convention's objective, in its own terms, is to prevent unnecessary delays in maritime traffic, to aid co-operation between Governments, and to secure the highest practicable degree of uniformity in formalities and other procedures. Three things are being pursued at once - speed, cooperation and uniformity - and limbs (b) and (c) of this question are simply those objectives examined in turn.

blocks.h: 3. Structure, and the Standards / Recommended Practices mechanism

blocks.p: The instrument is in two parts: the Articles, which bind the Contracting Governments as a treaty, and the Annex, which carries the operative facilitation measures. The Annex divides its measures into two classes, and the distinction is the mechanism that makes the Convention work:

ul: a Standard is a measure that is necessary and practicable for facilitating international maritime traffic. A Government which finds it impracticable to comply, or which applies a different measure, must notify the Secretary-General of the difference. That obligation is what stops non-compliance being silent.
a Recommended Practice is a measure it is desirable to apply. Here notification runs the other way - a Government is asked to notify when it brings its practice into full accord.

blocks.p: So the Convention neither imposes uniformity by force nor leaves it to goodwill. It creates a published record of every divergence, which is a far more workable instrument for a subject where port procedure is bound up with national customs and immigration sovereignty.

blocks.h: 4. The Annex sections and the FAL Forms

blocks.p: The Annex is arranged in seven sections: definitions and general provisions; arrival, stay and departure of ships; arrival and departure of persons; stowaways; arrival, stay and departure of cargo and other articles; public health and quarantine, including sanitary measures for animals and plants; and miscellaneous provisions. Three appendices carry the maximum information that may be required, the exceptional paper declarations and the stowaway material.

The most visible provision is the standardised set of IMO FAL Forms - the General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, Crew's Effects Declaration, Crew List, Passenger List and the Dangerous Goods Manifest, supplemented since 2016 by further clearance documents. The governing principle is maximum information: a public authority may ask for no more than the Convention permits.

blocks.h: 5. Efficiency, and why security is served rather than sacrificed

blocks.p: Efficiency. A single standard data set, submitted once, removes duplicated declarations across a voyage; pre-arrival submission moves clearance off the critical path so that formalities are settled before the ship is on the berth; and a maximum-information rule caps what any authority may demand. Since the 2016 amendments, in force 1 January 2018, electronic exchange of that information has been mandatory from 9 April 2019, which converted the saving from paper handling to data handling.

Security. The instinctive answer - that facilitation and security pull against each other - is the wrong one, and saying why earns the mark. Standardised, structured, electronic data is more amenable to screening than a stack of differently formatted paper forms: crew and passenger lists arriving pre-arrival in a known format can be checked against watch lists before the ship berths; the cargo declaration and the dangerous goods manifest support risk-based targeting; and the Convention's provisions on stowaways address a security and humanitarian problem directly. The Convention also carries the ISPS-related security information within the same pre-arrival machinery. Facilitation done properly gives the authorities better information earlier, which is what security actually needs.

blocks.h: 6. Why a facilitation treaty produces cooperation and standardization

blocks.p: Standardization here is not an aspiration in the preamble; it is built into the machinery. The maximum-information rule caps demands; the FAL Forms fix the format; the notification of differences makes every divergence visible and therefore negotiable; and the IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business supplies an agreed data model so that the same fact carries the same name in every system. At FAL 46 five further data sets were added to the Compendium, covering ship reporting systems, certificates, registry details, inspections and port State control history.

The commercial significance follows. A common data set is what allows a port community system in one country to speak to a customs system in another; it lowers the entry cost for developing States, which need to build one interface rather than many; and it aligns the maritime leg with the wider single-window movement in trade facilitation, so that the ship is not the odd link in an otherwise digital chain.

blocks.h: 7. The position at this sitting - the single window is already mandatory

blocks.p: This is the currency of the question. The 2022 amendments, resolution FAL.14(46), adopted 13 May 2022, entered into force on 1 January 2024 - days before this examination. They make it mandatory for public authorities to establish, maintain and use single window systems for the electronic exchange of information required on the arrival, stay and departure of ships, and to combine or coordinate transmission so that information is submitted only once and re-used to the maximum extent possible. They also require Contracting Governments to allow ships and ports to remain fully operational during a public health emergency of international concern, with seafarers and port workers designated key workers irrespective of nationality or flag - the codified lesson of the crew-change crisis - and they introduce a systemic approach to corruption at the ship-shore interface, requiring authorities to assess the risk and develop preventive measures.

Note the amendment position precisely, because it is where marks are lost. The next amendments, resolution FAL.15(47), were adopted on 17 March 2023 but do not enter into force until 1 January 2025. At this sitting they are adopted but not in force. Amendments to the Annex are made by tacit acceptance under Article VII(2)(b): they take effect on the stated date unless at least one third of Contracting Governments object beforehand, which is what allows a technical annex to keep pace with practice.

The printed marks are 6 + 4 + 6 and the three limbs are not three separate topics - they are the Convention's three objectives examined in turn. Limb (a) is the instrument; limb (b) is speed; limb (c) is cooperation and uniformity. Recognising that turns a vague-looking discussion question into a structured one, and it stops the same material being written three times.

Limb (a) carries six marks and hides four tasks - what the Convention is, its objective, its structure, and its concrete provisions. Splitting it across four short route steps is what stops the six marks disappearing into one paragraph about reducing paperwork. Limb (b) is only four marks: two on efficiency, two on security, and the security half is the half candidates get wrong.

blocks.h: The single window is ALREADY mandatory at this sitting

blocks.p: This is the highest-value fact in the question and it is date-critical. Resolution FAL.14(46) entered into force on 1 January 2024. A candidate sitting this paper is sitting in the first month of the mandatory maritime single window.

Writing "the single window will become mandatory", or "is being introduced", is wrong at this date. So, in the other direction, is presenting the 2023 amendments as operative: FAL.15(47) was adopted 17 March 2023 but did not enter into force until 1 January 2025. Adopted is not in force. A candidate who states both dates correctly demonstrates exactly the distinction the examiners test across this whole syllabus.

blocks.h: Facilitation versus security - the argument to make

blocks.p: Limb (b) invites the answer that facilitation and security are in tension and must be balanced. That answer scores something, but the better one is that well-designed facilitation improves security. The reason is concrete: security screening is a data problem, and the Convention delivers a standard data set, submitted electronically, before arrival. Watch-list checks on crew and passenger lists, targeting from the cargo declaration and dangerous goods manifest, and stowaway procedures all depend on getting structured information early. Twenty different paper formats arriving at the gangway is worse for security, not better.

The honest qualification, which is worth adding, is that a single window concentrates data and therefore concentrates risk - which is exactly why FAL 46 also approved guidelines on the authentication, integrity and confidentiality of single window exchanges. Naming that shows the tension has been thought about rather than waved away.

blocks.h: Standards and Recommended Practices - get the notification direction right

blocks.p: This is a precision point that separates candidates. For a Standard, a Government notifies the Secretary-General when it cannot comply or applies something different. For a Recommended Practice, it notifies when it does bring its practice into full accord. The two run in opposite directions, and the reason is structural: the Convention wants divergence from Standards to be visible, and convergence towards Recommended Practices to be visible. Getting the direction backwards is a common and easily avoided error.

ul: Writing the single window as a future or forthcoming requirement. It became mandatory on 1 January 2024.
Presenting the 2023 amendments as in force. They were adopted 17 March 2023 and entered into force 1 January 2025 - after this sitting.
Reversing the notification duty for Standards and Recommended Practices.
Treating facilitation and security as simple opposites, and never explaining how standardised electronic data actually helps screening.
Confusing the FAL Convention with the ISPS Code or with SOLAS chapter XI-2. FAL governs formalities; ISPS governs security measures.
Quoting a number of Standards and Recommended Practices. The 2022 amendments followed a comprehensive review of the whole Annex and circulating counts are unreliable.
Forgetting that the Annex caps what may be demanded - the maximum-information rule is a provision, not a courtesy.

"Is the FAL Convention mandatory?" The Convention binds Contracting Governments. Within the Annex, Standards are binding subject to the duty to notify differences; Recommended Practices are not. Say which layer you mean.
"Who does the FAL Convention regulate?" Primarily public authorities, not the ship. It limits what the shore may demand. That is unusual among IMO instruments and is worth stating.
"Name the FAL Forms." General Declaration, Cargo Declaration, Ship's Stores Declaration, Crew's Effects Declaration, Crew List, Passenger List, Dangerous Goods Manifest.

"What did the pandemic change in the Convention?" The 2022 amendments require ships and ports to remain fully operational during a PHEIC and designate seafarers and port workers as key workers regardless of nationality or flag.
"How are the amendments made?" Tacit acceptance under Article VII(2)(b) - they enter into force on the stated date unless one third of Contracting Governments object first.
"What is the Compendium?" The IMO Compendium on Facilitation and Electronic Business - the agreed data model that makes single windows interoperable. FAL 46 added five data sets to it.
When was FAL adopted and when did it enter into force? Adopted 9 April 1965, in force 5 March 1967.
What is a single window, and when did it become mandatory? A single point of electronic submission for arrival, stay and departure information, mandatory from 1 January 2024 under FAL.14(46).
What does "once-only" mean? Information is submitted once and re-used to the maximum extent possible, rather than being asked for again by each authority.
Name the seven sections of the Annex.
What is the difference between a Standard and a Recommended Practice, and who notifies what?
Does electronic submission remove the need for paper entirely? Exceptional paper declarations are still provided for in the appendices.

blocks.p: The Convention's own objective gives the whole answer its spine: speed, cooperation, uniformity. Limb (b) is speed. Limb (c) is cooperation and uniformity. Limb (a) is the machinery that delivers all three.

For the Annex sections, walk the ship through the port in order: ship, people, stowaways, cargo, health - with definitions in front and miscellaneous behind. For the two classes of measure, remember that a Standard is Shall-strength and you report when you cannot meet it.

Limb (b) asks for its effect on two things that are usually presented as opposed, efficiency and security, for four. Limb (c) asks why it matters to global cooperation and standardization, for six. The three limbs map onto the Convention's own three stated objectives, which is the structural insight the question is built on.

blocks.h: 1. Where CII sits in law, and to whom it applies

blocks.p: The Carbon Intensity Indicator is regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, introduced by the 2021 revised Annex VI (resolution MEPC.328(76)), which entered into force on 1 November 2022. It is the operational half of the short-term GHG measure; EEXI, regulation 23, is the technical half. EEXI is assessed once against the ship's design; CII is assessed every year against how the ship is actually run.

It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above falling into the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1. Under regulation 28.1 the ship calculates its attained annual operational CII after the end of calendar year 2023 and after the end of each following calendar year, over the period 1 January to 31 December, using the fuel oil consumption data already collected under regulation 27 (the IMO DCS, running since calendar year 2019). Under regulation 28.2 it reports that value to its Administration within three months of the year end.

So at the date of this examination the position is precise: 2023 was the first calculation year, the first attained CII falls due for reporting by 31 March 2024, and no ship has yet been assigned a CII rating.

blocks.h: 2. The mechanism - attained, required, Z and the reference line

blocks.p: The rating is a comparison, not an absolute measurement. Three quantities are needed.

ul: Attained annual operational CII - what the ship actually achieved. In its simplest form it is the ratio of the total mass of CO2 emitted, M, to the total transport work undertaken, W, in the calendar year. M is derived from the DCS fuel figures using the fuel-to-CO2 conversion factors.
Required annual operational CII - the target. Regulation 28.4: Required CII = (1 − Z/100) × CIIR.
CIIR is the reference value for the ship type, set on the 2019 reference line under the G2 guidelines, resolution MEPC.353(78).

blocks.h: 3. The rating, and what attaches to it

blocks.p: Under regulation 28.6 the attained CII is verified against the required CII to give a rating of A, B, C, D or E - major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior - and the middle point of rating level C is the required annual operational CII itself. The G4 guidelines, resolution MEPC.354(78), place four boundaries around that midpoint - superior, lower, upper and inferior - for each year from 2023 to 2030.

The teeth are in regulations 28.7 to 28.9. A ship rated D for three consecutive years, or rated E in any single year, must develop a plan of corrective actions; the SEEMP is reviewed to incorporate it and submitted to the Administration for verification no later than one month after reporting the attained CII; and the ship must then duly undertake those actions. Regulation 28.10 works the other way, encouraging Administrations, port authorities and other stakeholders to provide incentives to ships rated A or B.

Note what the regulation does not do. There is no detention, no fine and no certificate withdrawn for a poor rating. The pressure is commercial - charterers, financiers and cargo owners read the rating - and administrative, through the SEEMP. Regulation 28.11 requires a review to be completed by 1 January 2026 covering, among other things, the need for reinforced corrective actions, enforcement, and revision of the Z and CIIR values. That review has not reported at this sitting.

blocks.h: 4. AER - what it measures and why the regulation uses it

blocks.p: The G1 guidelines, resolution MEPC.352(78), draw the distinction the question is really about. A demand-based CII uses the actual mass or volume of cargo carried. A supply-based CII uses the ship's capacity as a proxy for cargo. AER - the Annual Efficiency Ratio - is the supply-based CII which uses DWT as the capacity; the variant using GT is cgDIST.
So AER is, in grams of CO<sub>2</sub> per deadweight-tonne-mile:

ul: numerator - total CO2 from all fuel consumed in the calendar year, from DCS data;
denominator - ship's capacity × total distance travelled, from DCS data;

capacity is DWT for bulk carriers, tankers, container ships, gas carriers, LNG carriers, general cargo ships, refrigerated cargo carriers and combination carriers, and GT for cruise passenger ships, ro-ro cargo ships including vehicle carriers, and ro-ro passenger ships.

blocks.p: Its virtue is entirely practical: every input is already reported, auditable and comparable. Nothing new has to be measured, and two sister ships can be compared on identical terms.

EEOI - the Energy Efficiency Operational Indicator - is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684 and measures CO2 per tonne of cargo actually carried per mile. It is the demand-based metric, and it is a truer measure of transport work: a ship that sails full has done more work than one that sails in ballast, and EEOI says so where AER does not.

Its status at this sitting must be stated exactly. EEOI is not the regulatory metric. G1 section 5 lists it - with EEPI, cbDIST and clDIST - among metrics encouraged to be used for trial purposes. It is voluntary. Regulation 28 is satisfied by the supply-based indicator.
The critical case against AER is real and should be made:

ul: it rewards distance, not cargo. Long ballast legs, and idle days at anchor burning fuel while travelling no distance, both worsen AER; steaming light on a long passage can improve it;

it is blind to utilisation. Two identical ships, one full and one half empty, score the same if they burn the same fuel over the same distance - so the metric cannot reward the commercially efficient operator;
it penalises short-sea and multi-port trades, where port time and manoeuvring are a large share of consumption and sea distance is small;
it can be gamed at the margin by slow steaming with more ships, which lowers each ship's AER while the cargo moves no more efficiently overall.

blocks.p: The case for choosing it anyway is equally real. EEOI needs cargo mass data that the DCS does not collect, that is commercially confidential, that is not verifiable by an Administration in the way DCS data is, and that is not comparable across trades - a car carrier, a container ship and a crude tanker cannot be ranked on tonne-miles. IMO therefore chose the metric that could be audited and enforced over the one that is conceptually correct. That trade-off - enforceability bought at the cost of validity - is the answer to "critically discuss", and regulation 28.11's inclusion of the CIIR and Z values in its review is the acknowledgement that it is not settled.

blocks.h: 6. Operational measures to improve the rating

blocks.p: Because AER is fuel over capacity-distance, only two things can be done: burn less, or travel further for it. Operational measures dominate because they are available now and cost little.

ul: Speed and voyage management. Consumption rises far faster than speed, so optimising speed to the required arrival time is the single largest lever. Just-in-time arrival converts waiting at anchor - which burns fuel and adds no distance - into a slower, cheaper passage.
Hull and propeller condition. Planned in-water cleaning and propeller polishing against measured performance, rather than to a calendar.
Trim and draught optimisation against the ship's own trim tables or CFD-derived guidance, and optimum ballast - carry no more than is needed.
Weather routeing to avoid added resistance, and autopilot tuning to cut rudder-induced drag.

Machinery and auxiliary load. Shut down surplus generators, use the shaft generator where fitted, run pumps and fans on variable frequency drives, manage cargo heating and inert gas use, and control accommodation HVAC and lighting load.
Reduce port and idle consumption - shore power where available, minimise boiler use, avoid unnecessary main engine running.

blocks.p: Technical retrofit. Low-friction and foul-release hull coatings; propeller retrofit or upgrade and energy saving devices such as ducts, fins and rudder bulbs; engine derating with engine or shaft power limitation; waste heat recovery; air lubrication; and wind assistance. Each must be justified for the specific ship and trade - none is universally worthwhile.
Fuel. Because the numerator is CO2 and not fuel mass, switching to a fuel with a lower carbon factor - LNG, methanol, or a biofuel blend - reduces attained CII directly for the same energy delivered.

Data and calculation. Two legitimate levers that are not fuel savings at all. First, DCS data quality: the attained CII is only as good as the reported fuel and distance figures, so flowmeter calibration, consistent bunker figures and correct noon-report distances matter directly to the rating. Second, the G5 interim guidelines, resolution MEPC.355(78), allow defined voyage adjustments - which deduct fuel and the associated distance for qualifying periods - and correction factors, which adjust the numerator or denominator, for cases such as ice conditions, ship-to-ship operations and refrigerated containers. G5 states the boundary itself: their use should in no way undermine the goal of reducing the carbon intensity of international shipping.

All of this is administered through the SEEMP. Under regulation 26.3 an affected ship's SEEMP had to include, on or before 1 January 2023, the calculation methodology, the required CII for the next three years, an implementation plan for achieving it, and a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement - and it is subject to verification and company audit. The SEEMP is where an examiner expects the measures above to live, not in a loose list.

The question is one unlimbed block of 16 marks setting three tasks - explain CII rating, critically discuss AER and EEOI, and list improvement measures - and the middle one is where the marks actually are. "Critically discuss" is not "describe": a candidate who defines AER and EEOI and stops has answered half of the highest-value limb.

Steps 1 to 3 build the mechanism, and they must come first because the AER discussion is meaningless without knowing that the rating is a comparison against a moving target. Steps 4 and 5 are the critical core. Steps 6 and 7 are the improvement measures, split operational from technical so that the answer reads as a plan rather than a shopping list - and the operational half comes first because it is what a ship's engineer actually controls.

blocks.h: At this sitting, no ship has a rating yet

blocks.p: This is the temporal point of the question and it is easy to get wrong from later material. Regulation 28.1 requires the attained CII to be calculated after the end of calendar year 2023, and regulation 28.2 gives three months to report it. So at a January 2024 sitting: 2023 is the first data year, the first reports are due by 31 March 2024, and no rating has yet been assigned to any ship.

The reduction factor for the current year is 7 %. Factors are set through 2026 only - 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023 to 2026 - and the years 2027 to 2030 are expressly left open in G3, to be strengthened in light of the regulation 28.11 review. That review must complete by 1 January 2026 and has not reported at this sitting. Any statement about what the review decided, or about a post-2026 Z value, is a later-sitting import and is wrong here.
The examiner's word is critically. The argument to make is that IMO chose an enforceable metric over a valid one.

EEOI is the better measure of what shipping is for - moving cargo. AER measures how far a hull travelled per tonne of CO2, regardless of whether it carried anything. But EEOI requires cargo mass, which is commercially confidential, is not collected by the DCS, cannot be verified by an Administration, and cannot be compared across ship types. AER's inputs are already reported, already audited and already comparable. So the regulation uses AER and the guidelines relegate EEOI to trial purposes under G1 section 5.

The honest closing point is that regulation 28.11 puts the CII<sub>R</sub> and Z values inside the scope of its own review, which is IMO conceding that the metric is provisional. A candidate who says that has genuinely criticised the scheme rather than listed its flaws.

blocks.h: AER and EEOI - the distinction in one line each

blocks.p: AER - supply-based; capacity is a proxy for cargo; capacity is DWT; every input comes from the DCS; this is the regulatory metric under regulation 28. cgDIST is the same idea with GT instead of DWT, used for cruise passenger, ro-ro cargo and ro-ro passenger ships. EEOI - demand-based; uses actual cargo carried; defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684; voluntary, for trial purposes.
The word to hold on to is proxy. AER's every strength and every weakness follows from substituting capacity for cargo.

ul: Saying ships already hold CII ratings at this sitting. 2023 is the first data year and the first reports are due 31 March 2024.
Giving the wrong reduction factor. For 2024 it is 7 %, relative to the 2019 reference line.
Asserting Z values for 2027 onwards. They were not set at this sitting.
Treating EEOI as a regulatory requirement. It is voluntary and, in G1, for trial purposes.
Confusing CII with EEXI. EEXI is technical and assessed once on design; CII is operational and assessed every year.
Saying a D or E rating leads to detention or a fine. The consequence is a corrective action plan in the SEEMP; the real pressure is commercial.
Saying a single D rating triggers corrective action. It is D for three consecutive years, or E.
Listing improvement measures with invented percentage savings. Quote mechanism, not vendor figures.
Forgetting that improving data quality and applying the G5 voyage adjustments are legitimate levers alongside burning less fuel.
"Where does rating C sit?" Regulation 28.6 - the middle point of rating level C is the required annual operational CII. C is not a pass mark, it is the target itself.
"What happens to a ship rated D?" Nothing, for one year, and for two. It is D for three consecutive years, or a single E, that triggers regulation 28.7.

"A ship waits three weeks at anchor. What does that do to AER?" It worsens it - fuel is burned and no distance is travelled, so the numerator grows and the denominator does not. It is the clearest illustration that AER measures distance, not work.
"How would EEOI treat the same three weeks?" The same way in the numerator, but EEOI at least credits the cargo actually carried on the voyage either side.

"Can a shipowner improve CII without touching the ship?" Yes - speed and voyage management, better DCS data quality, and the G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors where the ship genuinely qualifies.
"Which guideline gives what?" G1 the indicators and calculation, G2 the reference lines, G3 the reduction factors, G4 the rating boundaries, G5 correction factors and voyage adjustments.
"Is CII in the SEEMP?" Yes - regulation 26.3, the SEEMP Part III content, required on or before 1 January 2023.
Which regulation is CII, and which Annex? Regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI.
Which ships does it apply to? Ships of 5,000 GT and above in the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1.
Write the required CII formula. Required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference.
What is the reference year for the reference line? 2019.
What is AER in words? Grams of CO2 per deadweight tonne-mile, using capacity as a proxy for cargo.
Where is EEOI defined and what is its status? MEPC.1/Circ.684; voluntary, for trial purposes.
Name three operational measures and one calculation measure to improve a rating.
When must the review of the measure be completed? By 1 January 2026, under regulation 28.11.

blocks.p: Hold the mechanism as three words in order: ATTAINED, REQUIRED, RATED. What the ship did, what it was supposed to do, and the letter that follows. Then the letter grades are simply the five words of regulation 28.6 - major superior, minor superior, moderate, minor inferior, inferior.

For the guidelines, count them in the order the calculation actually runs: G1 how to calculate it, G2 what to compare it to, G3 how much to tighten it, G4 how to grade it, G5 what may be adjusted. For the reduction factors, the odd numbers climb by two - 5, 7, 9, 11 for 2023, 2024, 2025, 2026 - and then stop.

For the improvement measures, work down the formula: the numerator is fuel and its carbon, the denominator is capacity and distance. Everything you can do is in one of those two places, or in the quality of the numbers themselves.

points: only two things are possible - burn less fuel, or travel further for it
speed optimisation and just-in-time arrival, converting waiting at anchor into a slower passage
hull cleaning and propeller polishing planned against measured performance, not the calendar
trim and draught optimisation, and carrying no more ballast than is needed
weather routeing to avoid added resistance, and autopilot tuning to cut rudder drag

questions.understand_first: CII does something none of the older MARPOL rules do: it grades how the ship is OPERATED, every year, and the pass mark moves. The ship's own fuel and distance figures, already reported to the flag State since 2019, are turned into a number; that number is compared with a target derived from the 2019 industry average and tightened by a percentage that grows each year; and the comparison produces a letter from A to E. Everything else follows. The reason AER and EEOI are worth arguing about is that the whole scheme rests on how you measure "transport work", and IMO deliberately chose the measure it could audit - capacity times distance - over the measure that is actually true - cargo times distance. And the reason the improvement measures list is not arbitrary is that the metric is a fraction: you can only attack the numerator, the denominator, or the quality of the numbers.
questions.memory_cue: The mechanism is three words in order - ATTAINED, REQUIRED, RATED (steps 1, 2, 3). The argument is two metrics - AER the enforceable one (4), EEOI the true one (5). The measures follow the fraction - numerator and denominator, operational first (6), then technical, fuel and data (7).

Required CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference, where the reference is the 2019 line and Z is 5, 7, 9, 11 per cent for 2023 to 2026 - 2027 onwards not yet set. Rating A to E; the middle point of C is the required CII. D for three consecutive years or E means a corrective action plan in the SEEMP within one month of reporting; incentives are encouraged for A and B. Review due by 1 January 2026. AER is the supply-based metric using DWT as a proxy for cargo - the regulatory one. EEOI, MEPC.1/Circ.684, uses actual cargo and is voluntary, for trial purposes. Improve by speed and voyage management, hull and propeller condition, trim and ballast, auxiliary load, retrofit and fuel switching, plus DCS data quality and the G5 adjustments.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which regulation is CII, where did it come from, and which ships does it catch?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 28 of MARPOL Annex VI, introduced by the 2021 revised Annex VI, resolution MEPC.328(76), in force 1 November 2022. It applies to ships of 5,000 gross tonnage and above falling into the cargo and passenger categories listed in regulation 28.1.
retrieval_cards.why: The regulation number and the tonnage threshold are the two cheapest marks in the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Write the required CII formula and give the reduction factors.
retrieval_cards.answer: Required annual operational CII = (1 - Z/100) x CII reference, where the reference value is on the 2019 reference line. Under G3, MEPC.338(76) table 1, Z is 5 % for 2023, 7 % for 2024, 9 % for 2025 and 11 % for 2026. The factors for 2027 to 2030 are to be further strengthened and developed and were not set.
retrieval_cards.why: Getting the current year's Z right is what shows the answer is anchored to its own sitting.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is AER, and what does it use as its denominator?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Annual Efficiency Ratio - the supply-based CII which uses deadweight tonnage as the capacity. The numerator is total CO2 from all fuel consumed in the calendar year; the denominator is the ship's capacity multiplied by the total distance travelled. The variant using gross tonnage instead of DWT is cgDIST.
retrieval_cards.why: Supply-based means capacity is a PROXY for cargo, and every strength and weakness of AER follows from that one substitution.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish AER from EEOI and state the status of each.
retrieval_cards.answer: AER is supply-based: it uses the ship's capacity as a proxy for cargo, takes every input from the IMO DCS, and is the metric by which regulation 28 is satisfied. EEOI is demand-based: it uses the cargo actually carried, is defined in MEPC.1/Circ.684, and under G1 section 5 is encouraged for trial purposes only. EEOI is voluntary.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the whole of the critical limb, and treating EEOI as mandatory is the commonest error in it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why did IMO regulate with AER when EEOI is the better measure of transport work?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because EEOI requires cargo mass data which the DCS does not collect, which is commercially confidential, which an Administration cannot verify as it verifies fuel and distance, and which is not comparable across ship types. AER's inputs are already reported, already audited and already comparable. IMO chose the enforceable metric over the valid one - and regulation 28.11 puts the reference values and Z factors inside its own review, which concedes the choice is provisional.
retrieval_cards.why: "Critically discuss" is asking for this trade-off, not for a list of AER's flaws.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What happens to a ship rated D, and what happens to one rated E?
retrieval_cards.answer: A single D does nothing. It is D for three consecutive years, or E in any one year, that triggers regulation 28.7: the ship develops a plan of corrective actions, the SEEMP is reviewed to include it and submitted to the Administration no later than one month after reporting the attained CII, and the actions must be duly undertaken. There is no detention, fine or certificate withdrawal.
retrieval_cards.why: The three-consecutive-years condition and the absence of a penal sanction are both routinely got wrong.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Where does rating C sit relative to the required CII?
retrieval_cards.answer: Regulation 28.6 - the middle point of rating level C is the value equivalent to the required annual operational CII. C is the target itself, not a pass mark below it.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains why the whole fleet cannot simply settle at C as the standard tightens.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the five CII guidelines and what each supplies.
retrieval_cards.answer: G1, MEPC.352(78) - the indicators and the calculation method. G2, MEPC.353(78) - the reference lines. G3, MEPC.338(76) - the reduction factors. G4, MEPC.354(78) - the rating boundaries. G5, MEPC.355(78) - correction factors and voyage adjustments.
retrieval_cards.why: They run in the order the calculation runs: calculate, compare, tighten, grade, adjust.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give three ways to improve CII that do not involve modifying the ship.
retrieval_cards.answer: Speed and voyage management, especially just-in-time arrival so that time waiting at anchor becomes a slower passage instead; improving the quality of the DCS fuel and distance data on which the attained CII is calculated; and applying the G5 voyage adjustments and correction factors where the ship genuinely qualifies, for example ice conditions or ship-to-ship operations. G5 adds that their use must in no way undermine the goal of reducing carbon intensity.
retrieval_cards.why: It shows the metric is a fraction with three attackable parts, not just a fuel bill.

retrieval_cards.prompt: A ship spends three weeks at anchor awaiting a berth. What does that do to its AER?
retrieval_cards.answer: It worsens it. Fuel is burned, so the numerator grows, while no distance is travelled, so the denominator does not. Time at anchor is pure penalty under AER.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the sharpest single illustration that AER measures distance covered, not work done.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What must an affected ship's SEEMP contain, and since when?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under regulation 26.3, on or before 1 January 2023: a description of the methodology for calculating the attained CII and the reporting process; the required annual operational CII for the next three years; an implementation plan documenting how it will be achieved; and a procedure for self-evaluation and improvement. The SEEMP is subject to verification and company audits.
retrieval_cards.why: The improvement measures belong inside this plan; listing them loose misses where the regulation puts them.

blocks.h: 1. What preventive maintenance is, and where it sits

blocks.p: Preventive maintenance is work done before a failure, on a plan, to keep equipment fit for service. It sits between two alternatives which are still used deliberately: corrective (breakdown) maintenance, acceptable only for non-critical items where failure is cheap and safe, and condition-based maintenance, where the intervention is triggered by measured condition rather than by elapsed time. A mature ship uses all three - the skill is allocating each item to the right one.
The elements below are a system, not a list of good intentions. Remove any one and the rest degrade.

ul: An equipment register with criticality ranking. Every item identified, and each one classified by the consequence of its sudden failure. This is what decides which strategy applies, and it is the same judgement the ISM Code requires at element 10.3.

A defined maintenance task for each item, on a defined trigger. The task comes from the maker's recommendations and class requirements as the baseline, refined by the ship's own experience. The trigger is running hours, calendar time, or measured condition.

Condition monitoring for the items that warrant it - lubricating oil analysis, vibration analysis, thermography, performance and pressure-temperature trending, wear-down measurement. Its purpose is to convert time-based overhaul into evidence-based overhaul.

Spares, stores and tools. Critical spares identified and held on board, minimum stock levels, and control of the special tools and lifting gear each job needs. A planned job with no spare is not planned.

Competent people and safe procedures - trained and familiarised staff, work planned around manning and rest hours, and the permit-to-work, isolation, enclosed-space and hot-work controls that the job actually requires.
Records and feedback. What was done, when, by whom, what was found, and what was renewed. Records are the evidence at survey and audit, and the raw material for revising intervals.
Review and improvement. Defect and failure analysis feeding back into the intervals and the tasks, so that the plan changes when the evidence says it should.

blocks.p: Behind all seven sits the Planned Maintenance System - normally a software system - which holds the register, raises the jobs, and keeps the records. The PMS is the tool; the elements above are the system it serves.

blocks.h: (b) Statutory survey, class survey, routine maintenance and the SMS
3. Statutory survey - what it is and who requires it

blocks.p: A statutory survey is required by an international convention or national law and is carried out by the flag Administration, or by a Recognized Organization to which the Administration has delegated the work under the RO Code. It leads to a statutory certificate - Safety Equipment, Safety Construction, Safety Radio, Load Line, IOPP, IAPP and the rest. Delegation is of function, not of responsibility: the Administration remains responsible for the certification of its ships.

The harmonized system of survey and certification aligns the survey dates and certificate validities so that one visit can serve several certificates. The current guidance is resolution A.1186(33), the Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, which revoked A.1156(32) and states that it takes account of instruments entering into force before or on 31 December 2023. It defines seven types of survey:

rows: Initial (I)
A complete inspection before the ship is put into service of all items relating to a particular certificate.
Annual (A)
A general inspection to ensure the items have been maintained and remain satisfactory.
Intermediate (In)
An inspection of specified items relevant to the certificate.
Periodical (P)
An inspection of the items to ensure they are in satisfactory condition and fit for service.
Renewal (R)
The same as a periodical survey, but it also leads to the issue of a new certificate.
Bottom (B)
Inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom and related items.
Additional (Ad)
General or partial, after important repairs or renewals, or after change or significant repair of structure, equipment or systems.

blocks.p: Note the wording of the annual survey - it asks whether the items have been maintained. The convention itself points at the maintenance record.

blocks.h: 4. Classification survey - and how the two differ

blocks.p: A classification survey is required by the society's own rules under a contract between owner and society. It verifies that hull, machinery and essential systems remain in accordance with class rules, and it maintains class - special (renewal) survey on a five-year cycle, annual and intermediate surveys within it, plus tailshaft, boiler and other item surveys on their own cycles. The outcome is not a legal certificate but the class notation, with any deficiency recorded as a condition of class or recommendation carrying a due date.

The distinction that carries the mark is one of authority, not of activity. Statutory survey is public law, owed to the flag State, and enforced by port State control and detention. Class survey is private contract, owed to the society, and enforced commercially - by insurers, charterers and financiers, for whom loss of class is fatal. The same surveyor from the same society often does both in the same attendance, which is exactly why candidates conflate them - but he wears two hats, one as the society and one as the RO.

blocks.h: 5. The mechanism that links routine maintenance to survey

blocks.p: The link is not merely that good maintenance makes surveys go well. It is structural.

Survey verifies condition; maintenance produces it. A surveyor attending an annual survey does not rebuild the ship - he samples, examines, witnesses tests, and reads the records. Where the maintenance system is sound the records are the evidence, and where it is not the survey is the point at which that becomes visible.

The formal instrument is the class-approved planned maintenance scheme. Instead of opening machinery for a surveyor on a fixed cycle, the owner submits the PMS for class approval; once approved, maintenance carried out by the ship's own chief engineer to the approved scheme, and properly recorded, is credited towards the machinery survey requirement, with the society confirming at an annual audit that the scheme is being followed. A condition monitoring scheme extends the same principle to evidence from vibration and oil analysis in place of opening up. The commercial consequence is real - surveys stop dictating the docking plan - and so is the obligation: the credit depends entirely on records that stand up.

The link also runs the other way. A defect found in routine maintenance may require notification to class, may generate a condition of class or an additional survey under A.1186(33) 2.7 after important repairs or renewals, and - where it affects a statutory item - may make the ship's certificate invalid until it is rectified.

blocks.h: 6. How the ISM Code merges it into the SMS

blocks.p: Element 10, Maintenance of the Ship and Equipment, is what converts all of the above from good practice into an auditable requirement. Its four paragraphs each do a distinct job:

ol: 10.1 - the Company shall establish procedures to ensure the ship is maintained in conformity with the relevant rules and regulations and with any additional requirements established by the Company. "Rules and regulations" is what pulls both class rules and statutory requirements inside the SMS; the final clause is what lets the Company set a standard above them.
10.2 - inspections at appropriate intervals; any non-conformity reported with its possible cause, if known; appropriate corrective action taken; and records maintained. That is the audit trail.

10.3 - the Company shall identify equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations, and the SMS shall provide specific measures to promote the reliability of such equipment, including the regular testing of stand-by arrangements and equipment not in continuous use. This is critical equipment, and it is the direct statutory root of the criticality ranking in limb (a).

10.4 - the inspections at 10.2 and the measures at 10.3 shall be integrated in the ship's operational maintenance routine. The Code expressly forbids running a separate safety inspection regime alongside the PMS.

blocks.p: The surrounding elements complete the loop. Element 9 requires non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences to be reported, investigated and analysed, with corrective action to prevent recurrence - which is where a repeated failure becomes a revised maintenance interval rather than a repeated repair. Element 11 controls the documents, so that the manual on board is the current one. Element 12 requires internal safety audits at intervals not exceeding twelve months, exceptionally extendable by not more than three, by auditors independent of the area audited.
Put end to end, the ship carries one maintenance process and three different bodies read it for three different purposes:

ul: the PMS plans and records the work, and criticality decides how much attention each item gets;
class reads those records at survey, and may credit them against the machinery survey where the scheme is approved;
the flag State or its RO reads the same evidence at statutory survey and issues or endorses the certificate;
the ISM audit reads the process itself rather than the machinery, and asks whether 10.1 to 10.4 are actually being done - leading to the SMC for the ship and the DOC for the Company;
port State control then tests the whole thing from the outside, and a pattern of maintenance-related deficiencies is treated as an ISM failure, not merely a machinery one.

blocks.p: That is the merger the question is asking about. Maintenance, class survey, statutory survey and audit are not four regimes bolted together; they are one body of evidence examined by four readers, and the ISM Code is the instrument that requires the evidence to exist.

The printed split is 6 + 10, and the ten-mark limb is the one that decides the answer. Limb (a) is a list question - two short steps, seven elements, done. The temptation is to write limb (a) at length because it is comfortable, and then run out of time on the limb worth almost twice as much.

Limb (b) uses the word analyse, not describe. It sets three tasks: distinguish the two survey regimes, connect them to routine maintenance, and show how the ISM Code absorbs both. Splitting it across four route steps - statutory, class, the linking mechanism, and element 10 - is what stops the answer becoming a general essay on the ISM Code. The closing step then shows the whole chain working, which is the actual analysis.

blocks.h: The linking mechanism is the point of the question

blocks.p: Most candidates can define a statutory survey and a class survey. Far fewer can name the mechanism that joins routine maintenance to survey, and that is where the analysis marks are.

The mechanism is the class-approved planned maintenance scheme: maintenance done by the ship's own chief engineer to a scheme the society has approved, and properly recorded, is credited against the machinery survey requirement, subject to an annual confirmation that the scheme is being followed. The condition monitoring scheme is the same principle using measured evidence instead of opening up. Say that, and the connection between limb (a) and limb (b) is made explicit rather than left for the examiner to infer.
The reason statutory and class survey are so often confused is that the same person from the same society frequently does both on the same attendance. The distinction is one of authority.

Class survey is private contract under the society's own rules, and its sanction is commercial - loss of class, and with it insurance and employment. Statutory survey is public law under a convention, carried out by the flag State or by a Recognized Organization acting under delegated authority, and its sanction is legal - an invalid certificate and detention at port State control. Delegation to an RO transfers the function, never the responsibility.

blocks.h: Element 10 - quote it, do not paraphrase it

blocks.p: Four short paragraphs carry most of limb (b)'s statutory content, and each does a different job. 10.1 procedures, in conformity with rules and regulations and any additional Company requirements. 10.2 inspections at appropriate intervals, non-conformity reported with its possible cause, corrective action, records. 10.3 critical equipment - identify what may fail suddenly and cause a hazardous situation, provide specific measures for reliability, including regular testing of stand-by arrangements not in continuous use. 10.4 integrate all of it into the ship's operational maintenance routine.

Two phrases are worth reproducing exactly because they show the Code has been read: "with its possible cause, if known" at 10.2.2, and "regular testing of stand-by arrangements and equipment or technical systems that are not in continuous use" at 10.3. The second is why the emergency generator, emergency fire pump and standby lubricating oil pump are tested on a routine - it is a Code requirement, not a habit.

ul: Writing limb (a) at length and leaving too little for the ten-mark limb.
Describing preventive maintenance as merely "maintenance at fixed intervals". Condition-based work is preventive too, and the criticality decision is the interesting part.
Saying class survey and statutory survey are the same thing because the same society does both.
Saying the Administration transfers responsibility to the RO. It delegates function only.
Treating ISM element 10 as generic quality-system language and never quoting it.
Omitting 10.3 - critical equipment and the testing of stand-by arrangements is the paragraph that connects the SMS to the engine room.
Missing 10.4 entirely. The Code requires integration into the operational maintenance routine, which is precisely what "effectively merged" in the question means.
Forgetting the PMS approval mechanism, which is the concrete link the question is asking for.
Quoting a class rule number. Class rules are society-specific.

"What is critical equipment, and where does the requirement come from?" ISM 10.3 - equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations. The measures must include regular testing of stand-by arrangements not in continuous use.

"Your PMS is approved by class. Does that remove the surveyor?" No. It credits the chief engineer's recorded work against the machinery survey requirement, subject to the society confirming annually that the approved scheme is being followed. It is a change of method, not an exemption.

"A pump is overhauled and the job is not recorded. What is the consequence?" Under ISM 10.2.4 the record is part of the requirement, so the non-conformity is in the system, not only in the pump. Under a class-approved scheme it may also cost the survey credit.
"Who issues the SMC and who issues the DOC?" The SMC is issued to the ship and the DOC to the Company, by the Administration or an organization recognized by it.

"What is an additional survey?" A.1186(33) 2.7 - general or partial, after a repair resulting from investigation or whenever important repairs or renewals are made, or after change, replacement or significant repair of structure, equipment, systems, fittings, arrangements and material.
"How does the annual survey relate to maintenance?" Directly. A.1186(33) 2.5 defines it as a general inspection to ensure the items have been maintained and remain satisfactory.
Name the seven types of survey in the harmonized system.
Which resolution carries the current HSSC Survey Guidelines? A.1186(33), adopted 6 December 2023, revoking A.1156(32).
What is the difference between a condition of class and a statutory deficiency?
How often are internal ISM audits required? At intervals not exceeding twelve months, exceptionally extendable by not more than three.
Must an internal auditor be independent? Yes - element 12.5, independent of the areas being audited.
Give three examples of critical equipment on your ship and say what specific measures the SMS provides for them.
What triggers an additional survey?

blocks.p: For limb (a), walk the life of a maintenance job: what have I got (register and criticality), what must be done and when (task and trigger), how do I know (condition monitoring), what do I need (spares, tools, people), what did I do (records), what did I learn (review). Six steps, seven elements.

For limb (b), hold three readers of one record: class reads it for the rules, the flag State reads it for the convention, the auditor reads it for the system. And for the survey types, the HSSC letters spell the cycle - I before service, then A, In, P, R through life, with B underneath and Ad when something happens.

questions.understand_first: Every ship is inspected by three different people who never coordinate their diaries: a class surveyor checking the society's rules, a flag State surveyor checking the conventions, and an auditor checking the management system. What the question is really asking is why that does not produce three separate maintenance regimes. The answer is that all three read the SAME thing - the ship's maintenance record - and the ISM Code is what obliges that record to exist and to be honest. Element 10 is only four paragraphs long, but it takes what a good chief engineer would do anyway and makes it a procedure, with identified critical equipment, reported non-conformities and kept records. Once that exists, class can even credit the chief engineer's own work against the machinery survey. Maintenance stops being preparation for survey and becomes the evidence at it.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is the life of a job: what I have, what to do and when, how I know, what I need, what I did, what I learned (1, 2). Limb (b) is THREE READERS OF ONE RECORD - class (4), flag State (3), auditor (6) - joined by the approved PMS (5) and closed at the end (7).

Class survey comes from the society's own rules under contract and maintains class, with conditions of class as its sanction. They are linked by the class-approved planned maintenance scheme, under which the chief engineer's recorded work is credited against the machinery survey. ISM element 10 merges it into the SMS: 10.1 procedures in conformity with rules and regulations, 10.2 inspections, non-conformity with possible cause, corrective action and records, 10.3 critical equipment and regular testing of stand-by arrangements, 10.4 integrate into the operational maintenance routine. Element 12.1 - internal audits not exceeding twelve months.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the essential elements of a shipboard preventive maintenance system.
retrieval_cards.answer: An equipment register with criticality ranking; a defined maintenance task for each item from maker's and class requirements; a defined trigger - running hours, calendar or measured condition; condition monitoring where it is warranted; spares, stores and tools with critical spares identified; competent people and safe working procedures; records and feedback; and review and improvement from defect analysis.
retrieval_cards.why: Criticality is first because it decides which strategy each item gets, and it is also the ISM 10.3 judgement.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish a statutory survey from a classification survey.
retrieval_cards.answer: A statutory survey is required by an international convention or national law and is carried out by the flag Administration or a Recognized Organization acting under delegated authority; it leads to a statutory certificate and its sanction is legal - an invalid certificate and detention. A classification survey is required by the society's own rules under contract with the owner; it maintains class, records deficiencies as conditions of class, and its sanction is commercial.
retrieval_cards.why: The same surveyor from the same society often does both in one attendance, which is why the two are conflated.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the seven types of survey in the harmonized system and the resolution that defines them.
retrieval_cards.answer: Initial, annual, intermediate, periodical, renewal, inspection of the outside of the ship's bottom, and additional. They are defined in resolution A.1186(33), Survey Guidelines under the HSSC, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023, which revoked A.1156(32).
retrieval_cards.why: The resolution number and its date show the answer is anchored to its own sitting - it was adopted one month before it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State ISM Code element 10.3.
retrieval_cards.answer: The Company should identify equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations. The SMS should provide for specific measures aimed at promoting the reliability of such equipment or systems, including the regular testing of stand-by arrangements and equipment or technical systems that are not in continuous use.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the paragraph that makes critical-equipment identification and stand-by testing a Code requirement rather than good practice.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does a class-approved planned maintenance scheme actually change?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maintenance carried out by the ship's own chief engineer to a scheme the society has approved, and properly recorded, is credited towards the machinery survey requirement instead of the machinery being opened for a surveyor on a fixed cycle. The society confirms annually that the approved scheme is being followed. A condition monitoring scheme extends the same principle to measured evidence.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the concrete link between routine maintenance and survey, and it is the analysis limb of the question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does ISM 10.4 require, and why does it matter to this question?
retrieval_cards.answer: That the inspections required by 10.2 and the measures required by 10.3 be integrated in the ship's operational maintenance routine. It matters because it forbids running a separate safety inspection regime alongside the PMS - integration is the Code's own word for what the question calls merging.
retrieval_cards.why: The question asks how maintenance is "effectively merged" into the SMS; 10.4 is the Code answering that in one line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How does A.1186(33) define an annual survey, and why is the wording significant?
retrieval_cards.answer: A general inspection of the items relating to the particular certificate to ensure that they have been maintained and remain satisfactory for the service for which the ship is intended. The words "have been maintained" point the surveyor directly at the maintenance record.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the textual proof that survey and routine maintenance are the same subject, not two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How often must internal ISM audits be carried out, and by whom?
retrieval_cards.answer: At intervals not exceeding twelve months, which in exceptional circumstances may be exceeded by not more than three months, under element 12.1. Under 12.5 the personnel carrying out audits should be independent of the areas being audited.
retrieval_cards.why: The three-month exceptional extension and the independence requirement are both commonly forgotten.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What triggers an additional survey?
retrieval_cards.answer: A.1186(33) section 2.7 - a repair resulting from investigations, or whenever important repairs or renewals are made; or change, replacement or significant repair of the structure, equipment, systems, fittings, arrangements and material.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the survey type that arises out of maintenance work itself, which is exactly the link the question is probing.
