blocks.h: (a) IACS structure, UR / UI / PR, and their significance
1. What IACS is and how it is organised

blocks.p: The International Association of Classification Societies is a non-governmental association of classification societies which holds consultative status at IMO. It makes no law. Its output is technical, and it reaches ships only through its Members' own rules or through Administrations choosing to rely on it.

ul: Council - the governing body, with one Council Representative per Member. It sets strategy, approves the budget, admits and suspends Members, and adopts Resolutions.

General Policy Group (GPG) - the executive deputy to Council, made up of Members' Permanent Representatives, which runs the work programme between Council sessions and approves technical Resolutions for implementation.

Panels and Expert Groups - the technical bodies which draft and revise the Resolutions, covering hull, machinery, survey, environmental and safety subjects, with further panels added as the Association's work has extended into decarbonisation and digitalisation.
Permanent Secretariat, in London, which administers the Association.
Quality Committee, which oversees Members' quality systems under the IACS quality system certification scheme - membership is conditional on meeting it.

blocks.p: No membership figure or panel count is given here deliberately: both have changed over time, and neither is needed to answer the question.

blocks.h: 2. UR, UI and PR - what each acts upon

blocks.p: All three are IACS Resolutions. They are distinguished not by subject but by what they act upon.

headers: What it acts upon, and its effect
rows: UR - Unified Requirement
A minimum technical requirement on a matter directly connected with class rules and practices.
Acts on the society's own Rules. Members must incorporate it into their Rules, normally within one year of GPG approval. It reaches a ship through class rules, never directly.
UI - Unified Interpretation
A common interpretation of a provision of an IMO instrument which is vaguely worded, or left to the satisfaction of the Administration.
Acts on an IMO convention. It secures uniform application across Members. It interprets; it does not create a class requirement.
PR - Procedural Requirement
A requirement about the Members' own procedures - how surveys are conducted, how class is transferred, how matters are reported.
Acts on the society itself. It governs how the society works, not the ship's technical standard.

blocks.p: The cleanest way to hold them apart is ship / convention / society: a UR ends up in the ship through the rulebook, a UI tells you what a convention means, and a PR disciplines the society.
The answer is yes, and the question is really asking for reasons rather than a yes.

ul: A UR is a floor. No Member's Rules may fall below it, so an owner gets a predictable technical standard whichever Member classes the ship - and cannot shop between societies for a materially softer rule. That is a benefit and a constraint at once: it also means a new UR can impose a real cost on an existing fleet.

A UI reduces regulatory risk. An arrangement accepted by one society is far less likely to be challenged by another Administration or at port State control if the interpretation is unified. That matters commercially, because the cost of a disputed interpretation is delay.

A PR has direct commercial bite. The procedural requirements on transfer of class prevent an owner escaping outstanding recommendations or conditions of class by moving society - the receiving society must take up the outstanding items.

blocks.p: There is a limit worth stating: IACS Resolutions bind Members, not owners. An owner classed with a non-IACS society is outside the system - which is itself a reason charterers and financiers care which society the ship is with.

blocks.h: (b) Recognized Organizations and the RO Code

blocks.p: A Recognized Organization is an organization to which a flag Administration has delegated authority to carry out statutory survey and certification work on its behalf - most commonly, but not necessarily, a classification society.

Two points carry the marks. First, the delegation is of function, not of responsibility: the Administration remains responsible for the statutory certification of its ships and cannot answer a casualty by pointing at its RO. Second, class society and RO are not synonyms. A society classes ships under its own rules as a commercial matter; it becomes an RO only where an Administration has delegated statutory work to it, only to the extent of that delegation, and only for that flag. The same society may be an RO for one flag and not another, and may hold different scopes from different flags. A surveyor attending one ship may therefore act in two distinct capacities in the same visit.

blocks.h: 5. The RO Code and its salient features

blocks.p: The Code for Recognized Organizations was adopted by resolution MSC.349(92) on 21 June 2013 and by resolution MEPC.237(65). Its purpose is to provide a harmonised, transparent and independent standard for assessing, authorising and overseeing ROs, so that a flag State's delegation is measured against a single international benchmark rather than each flag's own judgement.

ul: Part 1 - general provisions: purpose, definitions and application.

Part 2 - mandatory requirements for the flag State and the RO: competence and qualification of surveyors and auditors, a quality management system, independence, the written authorization agreement, and reporting duties.
Part 3 - guidelines for the oversight of ROs by flag States.
Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory; Part 3 is guidance. That distinction is examinable and is often got wrong.
It was made mandatory from 1 January 2015 by resolutions MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), amending SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol.

blocks.p: Note the pattern - a Code drafted as a standard, made binding by amending the conventions that refer to it. It is the same technique used for the III Code, and recognising it is worth a mark in an oral.
Monitoring runs on three levels.

Before delegation. The Administration determines that the organization has adequate technical, managerial and research capability; assesses it against the Code; and puts the delegation into a formal written agreement which defines the scope and limits of the authority conferred, the applicable national law and interpretations, the instructions to be followed where a ship is found unfit to proceed to sea, and the records to be kept.

During delegation. Periodic audit of the RO's quality management system; verification that surveyors and auditors are qualified to the Code's standard; vertical contract audits and witnessed surveys, in which the Administration follows a certificate back through the evidence or attends alongside the RO's surveyor; monitoring of performance indicators, principally port State control detentions and casualties attributable to certificates issued under the delegation; and a requirement that the RO refer any matter outside its delegated scope back to the Administration.

Sanction and audit of the Administration itself. The Administration may restrict, suspend or withdraw the authorization. And the Administration's own performance in doing all of this is not unexamined: under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme, the flag State is audited against the III Code, whose Part 2 requires an oversight programme for delegated authority, and against the obligations listed in resolution A.1187(33), adopted 6 December 2023. So the chain is complete - the RO answers to the Administration, and the Administration answers to IMO.

The printed split is 8 + 8 and each limb contains three tasks, so there are six things to answer and roughly two and a half marks each. That arithmetic decides the shape: nothing gets a long paragraph.

In limb (a) the organisation chart is the least valuable of the three tasks and is the one candidates write at greatest length. Give it a short bulleted list and put the marks into the UR/UI/PR distinction - a three-row table does that faster and more clearly than prose - and then answer the "does it have significance" task with a reasoned yes and concrete consequences. An answer that lists the three acronyms without distinguishing their status has not answered the question that was set.

In limb (b) the three tasks are roughly equal. The definition of an RO is short; the RO Code's features are a structured list; the oversight limb is where an answer can show real understanding by organising it as before, during and sanction rather than as an undifferentiated list of activities.
All three IACS Resolutions look alike on the page. They differ in what they act upon.

A UR acts on the society's Rules - it is a technical floor the Member must write into its own rulebook, which is why a UR reaches a ship only through class rules and never directly. A UI acts on an IMO convention - it says what an ambiguous SOLAS or MARPOL provision should be taken to mean, particularly where the convention leaves something to the satisfaction of the Administration. A PR acts on the society itself - how it surveys, reports and transfers class.
Ship / convention / society. Three words, and the distinction holds.

blocks.h: Classification society is not a synonym for Recognized Organization

blocks.p: A society classes ships under its own rules as a commercial matter between itself and the owner. It becomes a Recognized Organization only where a flag Administration has delegated statutory work to it, only to the extent of that delegation, and only for that flag.

The consequences are practical. The same society may be an RO for one flag and not another; it may hold a different scope from each; a surveyor may act in two capacities during one attendance; and a matter outside the delegated scope must be referred back to the Administration rather than decided by the society. Above all, the Administration keeps the responsibility - delegation moves the work, not the accountability.

ul: Describing a UR as directly binding on ships. It binds Members to amend their Rules.
Treating a UI as a class requirement rather than an interpretation of an IMO instrument.
Forgetting PRs entirely. They are the third of the three and carry marks - and transfer of class is the example that shows why they matter commercially.
Saying the RO Code is mandatory in its entirety. Parts 1 and 2 are mandatory; Part 3 is guidance.
Saying the Administration transfers responsibility to the RO. It delegates function only.
Saying IACS makes rules that ships must follow. IACS makes Resolutions that its Members must implement.
Quoting a number of IACS Members, or a fixed number of Panels. Both have changed and neither is required.
Answering the oversight limb with a single sentence about audits. It is worth roughly two and a half marks and has a structure - before, during, and sanction.

"If a UR and your flag State's national requirement conflict, which prevails?" The statutory requirement of the flag State. Class rules cannot override a statutory requirement; the RO acts only within the scope delegated to it and must refer anything outside that scope back.

"Who is responsible if an RO issues a certificate to a substandard ship?" The Administration remains responsible for the statutory certification. It may have recourse against the RO under the authorization agreement, and its own oversight will be examined - including under the Member State Audit Scheme.
"Which parts of the RO Code are mandatory?" Parts 1 and 2. Part 3 is guidelines for oversight.
"How long do Members have to bring a UR into their Rules?" Normally one year from GPG approval - but the GPG sets the period for a given Resolution, so "normally" is the safe word.
"Is a UI binding on an Administration?" No. It is a common interpretation among IACS Members. An Administration may adopt it, and many do, but it derives no authority from IACS.

"An owner wants to change class with outstanding conditions of class. Can he?" Not to escape them - the IACS procedural requirements on transfer of class require the outstanding items to be taken up by the receiving society.
"Who audits the Administration?" IMO, under the Member State Audit Scheme, against the III Code and the obligations listed in A.1187(33).
Which resolutions adopted the RO Code? MSC.349(92), of 21 June 2013, and MEPC.237(65).
When did it become mandatory, and under which instruments? 1 January 2015, under SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol, by MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65).
Which parts of the Code are mandatory? Parts 1 and 2.
What is the GPG and how does it relate to Council? The General Policy Group - the executive deputy to Council, made up of Members' Permanent Representatives.
Give one example of each of a UR, a UI and a PR in terms of what it acts upon.
Name three things the written authorization agreement must define.

How would an Administration detect a poorly performing RO? Principally through port State control detentions and casualties traceable to certificates issued under the delegation, and through audits and witnessed surveys.

blocks.p: For the three Resolutions - ship / convention / society. UR reaches the ship through the Rules; UI interprets the convention; PR governs the society. Say those three words to yourself and the table writes itself.
For the RO Code - 1 general, 2 mandatory, 3 oversight guidance. The part number is the memory hook: Part 2 is the one with teeth.

For the oversight limb - before, during, sanction. Before: assess and agree in writing. During: audit, qualify, witness, monitor detentions. Sanction: restrict, suspend or withdraw - and then IMSAS audits the Administration itself.

ul: IACS - Council, General Policy Group, Panels and Expert Groups, Permanent Secretariat, Quality Committee. Consultative status at IMO; no law-making power.
UR - Unified Requirement; minimum technical requirement; incorporated into Members' Rules, normally within one year of GPG approval.
UI - Unified Interpretation; common interpretation of an IMO instrument provision.
PR - Procedural Requirement; governs Members' own procedures, including transfer of class.
RO Code - adopted by res. MSC.349(92) (21 June 2013) and res. MEPC.237(65). Part 1 general, Part 2 mandatory, Part 3 oversight guidelines.
Mandatory from 1 January 2015 by res. MSC.350(92), MSC.356(92) and MEPC.238(65), under SOLAS, MARPOL Annexes I and II and the 1988 Load Line Protocol.
III Code, res. A.1070(28), and the IMO Member State Audit Scheme - the audit of the Administration's own oversight programme.
Res. A.1187(33) (6 December 2023) - the obligations list current at this sitting.

questions.understand_first: Two organisations sit between the flag State and the ship, and the question is testing whether you can tell them apart. IACS is a club of classification societies. It has no legal power at all: everything it produces reaches a ship either because a Member wrote it into its own rulebook, or because an Administration chose to adopt its reading of a convention. A Recognized Organization is something else entirely - it is a society doing the flag State's own statutory job under a written delegation, and only within whatever scope that delegation gives it. The RO Code exists because flags were delegating that job on wildly different terms, so IMO wrote one standard for assessing, authorising and overseeing the organisations doing it. Hold on to two ideas and both limbs answer themselves: IACS Resolutions act on the RULES, the RO Code acts on the DELEGATION - and neither ever moves the Administration's responsibility.

blocks.h: 1. What tribology is, and where it bites on board

blocks.p: Tribology is the science of friction, wear and lubrication between surfaces in relative motion. On a ship it is not an abstraction - it decides the condition of the cylinder liner and piston rings, the main, crankpin and crosshead bearings, the camshaft and gearing, the stern tube, and every deck machinery bearing on board.

The engineering aim in each of those contacts is to hold a full hydrodynamic film where possible, and to survive boundary and mixed lubrication where it is not - at top and bottom dead centre, at start-up, and at low load. Almost every development below is an attempt to widen the conditions under which the film survives, or to make the surfaces tolerant of the moments when it does not.

blocks.h: 2. The fuel change since 2020, and what it did to cylinder oil

blocks.p: The most consequential recent development in marine tribology was not a lubricant at all - it was a fuel regulation. Since 1 January 2020, MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 has imposed a global sulphur limit of 0.50 % m/m, and 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.
The consequences reach straight into the cylinder:

ul: Base number selection is now a decision, not a default. Cylinder oil alkalinity exists to neutralise sulphuric acid formed from fuel sulphur. Burn a compliant low-sulphur fuel on a high-BN oil and the surplus alkaline additive is not consumed - it deposits, giving hard calcium-rich deposits, bore polish and scuffing. Burn a high-sulphur fuel behind a scrubber on a low-BN oil and the acid is not neutralised - giving cold corrosion and rapid liner wear. Both failures are now live on the same fleet.
Two-oil and blending-on-board arrangements became mainstream, letting the BN delivered to the cylinder be varied with the fuel actually in use rather than fixed at a bunkering decision.

VLSFOs are blends, and they vary. Stability and compatibility between bunkers, wax appearance and sludging all became operational concerns, and a fuel that drops asphaltenes fouls the purifier and eventually the cylinder.

Catalytic fines - aluminium and silicon from refinery catalyst - remain the classic abrasive. They embed in the running surfaces and cut, and the defence is entirely mechanical: settling, purification at the right throughput and temperature, and drain checks.

blocks.p: The second development is the move from mechanical, camshaft-driven lubricators to electronically controlled timed injection. The oil is delivered as a metered quantity, timed to a specific crank angle so that it lands on the ring pack rather than the liner wall generally, and distributed through the quills at the moment the rings pass.

That control makes feed-rate optimisation possible. Dosing is set proportional to engine load and to fuel sulphur, and then trimmed against evidence - which is where limb two of this question joins limb one. The evidence is scrape-down (drip) oil analysis: oil collected from the piston underside and tested for iron content, which indicates wear, and residual base number, which indicates whether alkalinity is being consumed or wasted. The feed rate is reduced until iron begins to rise, and then set back. Lubrication has become a measured, closed-loop process rather than a fixed setting.
If the film cannot always be maintained, the surfaces must tolerate its loss. Hence:

ul: Liner surface engineering - plateau honing to give a bearing surface carrying oil-retaining grooves; hardened and thermally sprayed or laser-clad running surfaces; and anti-polishing rings at the top of the liner, which scrape the carbon crown from the piston and prevent the bore polishing that destroys the honing pattern.

Coated piston rings - chromium-ceramic and thermally sprayed coatings, and low-friction hard coatings including diamond-like carbon on smaller, higher-speed components, to raise scuffing resistance and cut boundary friction.
Bearing materials - tri-metal and polymer-overlaid bearings which tolerate thinner films, misalignment and momentary contact better than traditional white metal alone.

Base oils and additives - higher-quality Group II and III base stocks with better oxidation stability, and improved detergent, dispersant and anti-wear chemistry. Nanoparticle additives are an active research direction in the tribology literature, not established shipboard practice, and should be described as such.

blocks.h: 5. Environmentally acceptable lubricants and the stern tube

blocks.p: The third driver is environmental rather than mechanical. Where a lubricated interface can discharge to the sea - stern tube, controllable-pitch propeller hub, stabilisers, thrusters, deck cranes - the industry moved to Environmentally Acceptable Lubricants, biodegradable and minimally toxic, driven principally by United States Vessel General Permit requirements for oil-to-sea interfaces.

That is a genuine tribological change, not a paper one. EALs are typically ester-based, which brings different seal compatibility, greater sensitivity to water - an ester that takes up water can hydrolyse - and different behaviour on mixing with mineral oil. The parallel development is the water-lubricated stern tube bearing, with polymer or composite staves, which removes the oil-to-sea interface entirely at the cost of a bearing operating in a far less forgiving lubricant.

The final development is that tribology has become measured continuously rather than assessed at overhaul: on-board test kits for BN, water and viscosity; shore laboratory spectrographic analysis; particle counting and ferrography to size and shape the debris rather than merely count metal; vibration analysis for bearing condition; and liner wear measurement and scavenge-port inspection as the physical cross-check. The point of all of it is to move from time-based overhaul to evidence-based intervention.

blocks.h: 7. The analysis report - physical and chemical tests

blocks.p: A used-oil report is read as a trend, not as a single number. One sample out of line is a sampling question; three samples moving in one direction is a machinery question. Take samples at the same point, at the same running condition, at a regular interval, and upstream of the purifier if the object is to see contaminants.

rows: Viscosity high
Oxidation from overheating or long service; heavy insolubles and soot in suspension; water emulsion; contamination with residual fuel.
Check oil cooler and system temperatures; increase purification; check for fuel ingress; renovate, and renew if it will not recover.
Viscosity low, flash point low
Dilution with fuel - a leaking fuel pump, injector or high-pressure pipe, or leaking sealing oil arrangements.
Find and stop the leak - pressure-test pumps and injectors and check seals. A low flash point is also a fire risk; renew the charge once the source is closed.
Water present
Cooler leak, jacket water leak, condensation in the sump, or sea water ingress. Test for chlorides or sodium to distinguish fresh water from sea water.
Locate the leak by pressure test; run the purifier as a clarifier or dehydrate; renew if emulsified or if sea water is confirmed, because chlorides drive corrosion and additive depletion.
Base number falling
Alkalinity consumed neutralising acid - high fuel sulphur, low feed rate, an under-alkaline grade, or blow-past of combustion products.
Verify fuel sulphur against the bunker delivery note; check cylinder oil grade and feed rate against the fuel in use; top up or renew. Investigate ring sealing if it recurs.
Base number rising in the system oil
Over-carry of alkaline cylinder oil into the crankcase, or excessive feed rate.
Review the feed rate and check stuffing box condition and drain arrangements.
Insolubles and soot high
Poor combustion - late or defective injection, fouled turbocharger or air cooler, overload, or blow-by past worn rings.
Check injection timing and injector condition, clean the air side, review load; increase purifier throughput; inspect through scavenge ports.
Oxidation or nitration high
High operating temperature, air entrainment, long service life, catalytic effect of wear metals.
Check cooler performance and sump aeration; shorten the analysis interval; renovate or renew.
Additive elements falling (Zn, P, Ca)
Additive depletion by service, by water washing, or by over-purification.
Review purifier settings and temperature; top up or renew - a depleted oil no longer protects even at correct viscosity.

blocks.h: 8. The analysis report - wear metals and contaminants

blocks.p: Spectrographic analysis reports the metals dissolved and finely suspended in the oil. Each one indicates where to look; the metallurgy of the particular engine governs, so the report narrows the search rather than closing it. A PQ index or ferrous debris monitor is read alongside, because spectrographic analysis under-reports the large particles that matter most.

rows: Iron (Fe)
Liner, piston rings, gearing, shafting, camshaft - the general wear indicator.
Correlate with scrape-down iron; inspect through scavenge ports; measure liner wear; review feed rate and cat-fine control.
Chromium (Cr)
Piston ring facing and plated surfaces.
Suspect ring wear or scuffing; inspect rings and liner surface at the next opportunity.
Copper (Cu)
Bearing overlay, bushes, and cooler tubes.
Distinguish the two - if water is also present, suspect the oil cooler; otherwise investigate bearings.
Lead and tin (Pb, Sn)
Bearing overlay and white metal.
Treat a rising trend seriously - check bearing temperatures and lube oil pressure, review filter and magnetic plug debris, and plan to open up.
Aluminium (Al)
Piston crowns and some bearing alloys - or catalytic fines.
Read with silicon. If Al and Si rise together in a broadly fixed ratio, it is cat fines, not component wear.
Silicon (Si)
Catalytic fines, airborne dust ingress, or silicone antifoam residue.
Check purifier throughput and temperature and settling tank drains; check air filtration; verify the fuel oil system is achieving separation.
Sodium (Na) and chlorides
Sea water ingress, or a sea-water-side cooler leak.
Locate the leak; renew the charge - sea water contamination is not recoverable by purification alone.

blocks.p: The discipline that makes all of this useful is simple to state and easily lost: act on trends, correlate the report with what the machine is telling you - filter debris, magnetic plug findings, bearing temperatures, scavenge-port inspection - and always find the source. Renewing the oil without finding the leak is the commonest wrong answer to a bad report.

The question prints as one 16-mark block and sets two tasks of unequal difficulty. "Latest developments in tribology" is open-ended and easy to waffle at; "inferences from a lub oil analysis report with the proposed corrective action in each case" is closed, specific, and where the reliable marks are.

So split the time roughly evenly but structure the two halves differently. The developments half is five named developments, each with a reason - not a general essay on friction. The analysis half is two tables, because the examiner has asked for a corrective action in each case and a table makes each pairing countable. A candidate who writes the analysis half as prose loses marks the table would have banked.

blocks.h: "Latest developments" - answer for the sitting you are in

blocks.p: This limb is sitting-relative by construction, and the honest way to handle it is to organise the developments around why they happened rather than around dates. The single largest driver at this sitting is the 2020 sulphur cap, and it is a genuinely tribological event: it changed what is burned, which changed what the cylinder oil has to neutralise, which reopened base number selection as a live engineering decision on every ship.

The second organising idea is that developments come in three families: the lubricant (base stocks, additives, EALs), the delivery (timed electronic dosing, feed-rate optimisation, blending on board), and the surfaces (honing, coatings, anti-polishing rings, bearing materials) - with measurement running underneath all three. Naming those families first turns an open question into a structured one.
One discipline: nanoparticle additives are research, not fleet practice. Mentioning them shows reading; presenting them as current shipboard technology does not.

blocks.h: The BN trap runs in both directions

blocks.p: This is the most examinable single idea in the developments half, and most candidates know only half of it.

Too little alkalinity for the sulphur burned gives cold corrosion: sulphuric acid condenses on the liner and corrodes it, and wear rates climb. That half is well known. Too much alkalinity for the sulphur burned is equally damaging: the calcium-bearing detergent is not consumed, so it deposits, giving hard deposits on the piston top land, bore polish and eventually scuffing. Since 2020 both failure modes exist in the same fleet at the same time, because a ship on compliant fuel and a scrubber-fitted ship on high-sulphur fuel need opposite oils. That is why blending on board and two-oil systems matter.

blocks.h: Read the report as a trend, and always find the source

blocks.p: Two rules carry the second half. A single sample is a sampling question; three samples moving together are a machinery question. And renewing the oil is not a corrective action - it is what you do after you have found the leak, the fouled cooler or the worn ring. An answer that proposes "change the oil" for every finding has not answered the question, which asks for the corrective action in each case.

The strongest single pairing to know is aluminium with silicon. Read alone, aluminium suggests piston or bearing material. Read with silicon, rising together in a broadly fixed ratio, it is catalytic fines - a fuel treatment problem, not a wear problem, and the corrective action is the purifier and the settling tanks, not the engine. Getting that right in an oral is worth more than reciting the whole table.

ul: Writing a general essay on friction and wear instead of naming developments and saying what drove them.
Missing the 2020 sulphur cap entirely. It is the largest tribological driver of the period and it is a regulation the candidate already knows.
Knowing only the cold-corrosion half of the base number problem and not the over-alkalinity half.
Presenting nanoparticle additives, or any laboratory development, as established shipboard practice.
Answering the second half in prose so that the inference and the corrective action are not visibly paired.
Proposing "renew the oil" as the corrective action for every finding, without finding the source.
Reading aluminium without silicon and diagnosing piston wear when the answer is catalytic fines.
Failing to distinguish fresh water from sea water when water is found - the chloride or sodium test decides the severity.
Quoting numeric limits, feed rates or BN grades from memory. They are maker-specific, and a wrong number is worse than none.

"Your system oil BN is rising. Is that good?" No. In the system oil it usually means over-carry of alkaline cylinder oil into the crankcase, or an excessive feed rate - review the feed rate and the stuffing box.
"Viscosity and flash point have both fallen. What is it?" Fuel dilution. Find the leaking injector, pump or high-pressure pipe. Note that it is also a fire risk, not only a lubrication one.
"Copper is rising. Which is it - bearings or cooler?" Look at the water content. Copper with water suggests the oil cooler; copper alone points at bearing overlay or bushes.
"How do you know the feed rate is right?" By scrape-down analysis - iron content and residual BN in the piston underside drain oil - not by the setting on the panel.

"What does an anti-polishing ring do?" It scrapes the carbon deposit from the piston top land at the top of the liner, preventing that deposit from polishing the bore and destroying the honing pattern that retains oil.

"Why can an EAL be more troublesome than mineral oil?" Ester base stocks bring different seal compatibility, greater sensitivity to water and possible hydrolysis, and different mixing behaviour with mineral oil.

"Spectrographic analysis shows low iron but the magnetic plug is loaded. Which do you believe?" Both - spectrographic analysis under-reports large particles, which is why a PQ index or ferrous debris monitor is read alongside it.
Define tribology and name four tribological contacts in your engine room.
What is the current global sulphur limit and since when? 0.50 % m/m since 1 January 2020, and 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas.
Why does a scrubber-fitted ship need a different cylinder oil from a ship on compliant fuel?
How would you set and then verify a cylinder oil feed rate?
Where do catalytic fines come from, what do they do, and how are they removed?
Name three tests you can carry out on board and three that need a shore laboratory.
Water is found in the crankcase oil. What is your sequence of actions?
What is the difference between spectrographic analysis and ferrography?

blocks.p: For the developments half, three families and one thread: LUBRICANT, DELIVERY, SURFACES - with MEASUREMENT running under all three. The fuel change sits above them as the driver.

For the analysis half, read the report in the order the laboratory prints it: physical, then chemical, then metals. Physical - viscosity, flash point, water. Chemical - base number, insolubles, oxidation, additives. Metals - Fe, Cr, Cu, Pb, Sn, Al, Si, Na.
For the metals themselves, group by what they accuse: Fe and Cr accuse the running gear; Cu, Pb and Sn accuse the bearings; Al with Si accuses the fuel; Na accuses the sea.

ul: MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14 - global sulphur limit 0.50 % m/m from 1 January 2020; 0.10 % m/m in emission control areas. The one hard regulatory anchor in this question.
MARPOL Annex VI regulation 18 - fuel oil quality, the bunker delivery note and the retained sample; the documentary route by which a fuel-related lubrication problem is traced.
United States Vessel General Permit requirements for oil-to-sea interfaces - the driver behind Environmentally Acceptable Lubricants.

Everything else in this answer is machinery engineering: maker's recommendations, oil supplier and laboratory practice, and classification-society technical material. Declared as engineering judgement under PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL section 2.1, not dressed up as regulation.

blocks.h: Uncertainty and the deliberate absence of numbers

blocks.p: No numeric wear limit, alarm threshold, feed rate, base number grade or oil change interval appears anywhere in this answer. Every one of those is maker-specific and installation-specific, and a general figure would be wrong for most ships. MIW requires an unverifiable quantity to be omitted rather than given false precision. The answer therefore gives the direction of each trend and what it indicts, which is what the question actually asks for and what an examiner can mark.

No percentage saving or friction reduction is attributed to any coating, additive or lubrication technology, for the same reason - those figures are vendor-sourced. Nanoparticle additives are declared as a research direction rather than fleet practice at this sitting.

The wear-metal attributions are indications, not identifications. They are the standard engineering reading and are sound, but the metallurgy of a particular engine governs, so the answer says the report narrows the search rather than closing it. The dominant provenance class of this question is engineering judgement, and that is stated rather than disguised.

questions.understand_first: Tribology sounds like a laboratory subject, but on a ship it is the difference between a liner that lasts and one that scuffs. Every lubricated contact is trying to keep a film of oil between two surfaces that want to touch, and the film is thinnest exactly where the loads are highest - at the top of the stroke, at start-up, at low load. The recent history of marine tribology is mostly the story of one regulation: when the sulphur cap changed the fuel in 2020, it changed the acid the cylinder oil has to neutralise, and suddenly choosing the wrong alkalinity could damage an engine in either direction. The second half of the question is the same subject seen from the other end. A used-oil report is the engine describing its own wear in chemistry, and the skill is not memorising a table - it is reading a trend, pairing elements that only mean something together, and remembering that changing the oil is what you do AFTER you have found what put the metal in it.
questions.memory_cue: The developments are three families with one thread - LUBRICANT, DELIVERY, SURFACES, all measured (2, 3, 4, 5, 6), driven by the fuel change (2). The report is read in the laboratory's own order - physical and chemical first (7), then the metals (8), where Fe and Cr accuse the running gear, Cu and Pb and Sn the bearings, Al with Si the fuel, and Na the sea.

quick_revision.recall_15s: Tribology is friction, wear and lubrication between surfaces in relative motion - liner and rings, bearings, gearing, stern tube. The driver of recent developments is the 0.50 % m/m global sulphur limit in force since 1 January 2020 under MARPOL Annex VI regulation 14. Base number selection is now a live decision: too little alkalinity gives cold corrosion, too much gives deposits, bore polish and scuffing - hence two-oil and blending-on-board systems. Delivery has moved to electronically controlled timed injection with feed rates optimised against scrape-down iron and residual BN. Surfaces have moved to plateau honing, hardened and coated liners, coated rings, anti-polishing rings and more tolerant bearing materials. Environmentally acceptable lubricants and water-lubricated stern tubes address oil-to-sea interfaces. Read a report as a TREND: viscosity and flash point down means fuel dilution; water needs a chloride test to separate fresh from sea; BN falling means acid attack, BN rising in the system oil means cylinder oil carry-over; insolubles mean combustion; Fe and Cr accuse the running gear, Cu and Pb and Sn the bearings, Al with Si means cat fines, Na means sea water. Always find the source before renewing the oil.

quick_revision.major_trap: Proposing "renew the oil" as the corrective action for every finding. The question asks for the corrective action in each case, which means finding the source - the leaking injector behind falling flash point, the cooler behind copper and water, the purifier behind aluminium and silicon. The paired trap is reading aluminium alone as piston wear when aluminium rising with silicon is catalytic fines, which is a fuel treatment problem and not a wear problem at all.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define tribology and name the main tribological contacts in a marine diesel installation.
retrieval_cards.answer: The science of friction, wear and lubrication between surfaces in relative motion. On board: cylinder liner and piston rings; main, crankpin and crosshead bearings; camshaft and gearing; the stern tube; and deck machinery bearings.
retrieval_cards.why: Naming the contacts turns an abstract definition into an engine-room answer in one line.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Why is cylinder oil base number selection a live decision since 2020?
retrieval_cards.answer: Because the sulphur cap changed the fuel. Alkalinity exists to neutralise sulphuric acid from fuel sulphur. Too little for the sulphur burned gives cold corrosion and rapid liner wear; too much is not consumed and deposits, giving hard deposits, bore polish and scuffing. A ship on compliant fuel and a scrubber-fitted ship on high-sulphur fuel need opposite oils, which is why two-oil and blending-on-board systems became mainstream.
retrieval_cards.why: Most candidates know the cold-corrosion half only; the over-alkalinity half is what distinguishes the answer.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How do you verify that a cylinder oil feed rate is correct?
retrieval_cards.answer: By scrape-down or drip oil analysis - oil collected from the piston underside and tested for iron content, which indicates wear, and residual base number, which indicates whether alkalinity is being consumed or wasted. The rate is reduced until iron begins to rise, then set back. The panel setting is not the evidence.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the point where the two halves of the question join - condition monitoring IS the lubrication control.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Viscosity and flash point have both fallen. What is the inference and the corrective action?
retrieval_cards.answer: Fuel dilution - a leaking fuel pump, injector or high-pressure pipe, or leaking sealing oil arrangements. Find and stop the leak by pressure-testing pumps and injectors and checking seals, then renew the charge. Note that a low flash point is a fire risk as well as a lubrication problem.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the cleanest inference on the report, and the fire-risk point is the one candidates omit.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Aluminium is rising in the analysis. What must you read it with, and why?
retrieval_cards.answer: With silicon. Aluminium alone suggests piston crowns or certain bearing alloys. Aluminium and silicon rising together in a broadly fixed ratio indicates catalytic fines - a fuel treatment problem, not component wear. The corrective action is then the purifier throughput and temperature and the settling tank drains, not the engine.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the single highest-value pairing on the report and the one that changes the corrective action completely.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Water is found in the crankcase oil. What is your sequence?
retrieval_cards.answer: Test for chlorides or sodium to distinguish fresh water from sea water. Locate the source by pressure test - oil cooler, jacket water leak, condensation or sea water ingress. Run the purifier as a clarifier or dehydrate. Renew the charge if the oil is emulsified or if sea water is confirmed, because chlorides drive corrosion and additive depletion and are not recoverable by purification alone.
retrieval_cards.why: The chloride test is what decides whether this is a nuisance or an oil change.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Copper is rising. How do you decide between bearings and the oil cooler?
retrieval_cards.answer: Look at the water content. Copper together with water suggests the oil cooler tubes; copper alone points to bearing overlay or bushes. Correlate with filter debris, magnetic plug findings and bearing temperatures before opening anything up.
retrieval_cards.why: One element with two very different origins, and the water result is what separates them.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which metals accuse which components?
retrieval_cards.answer: Iron and chromium accuse the running gear - liner, rings, gearing, shafting, plated surfaces. Copper, lead and tin accuse the bearings - overlay, white metal and bushes. Aluminium with silicon accuses the fuel, as catalytic fines. Sodium and chlorides accuse the sea.
retrieval_cards.why: Four groups instead of eight elements, which is what makes the table recallable under pressure.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Spectrographic analysis shows low iron but the magnetic plug is loaded with debris. Which do you believe?
retrieval_cards.answer: Both. Spectrographic analysis under-reports large particles, so a serious wear event can be in progress with a low spectrographic iron reading. That is why a PQ index or ferrous debris monitor is read alongside it, and why filter and magnetic plug findings are correlated with the report.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the limitation of the laboratory method, and knowing it prevents a false reassurance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is an anti-polishing ring and what does it prevent?
retrieval_cards.answer: A ring fitted at the top of the cylinder liner which scrapes the carbon deposit from the piston top land. It prevents that deposit from polishing the bore, which would destroy the honing pattern that retains the oil film and lead to increased wear and scuffing.
retrieval_cards.why: A concrete piece of surface engineering that shows the developments limb has been answered with real content.

blocks.h: (a) The concept, its significance, and its effect on safety culture
1. What vetting is, and what it is not

blocks.p: Vetting is a commercial risk assessment carried out by a charterer, oil major or terminal operator to decide whether it is prepared to employ a particular tanker for a particular cargo on a particular voyage. It is entirely voluntary in law and is enforced by the market rather than by an Administration.
The distinction from everything else that inspects a tanker is worth stating precisely, because it is the concept the question is asking about:

ul: Statutory survey asks: does the ship comply with the conventions? The sanction is legal - an invalid certificate.
Classification survey asks: does the ship comply with class rules? The sanction is loss of class.
Port State control asks: is this ship substandard, here and now? The sanction is detention.
Vetting asks a different question altogether: am I willing to put my cargo, my terminal and my reputation behind this ship and this crew? The sanction is that the ship does not get the fixture.

blocks.p: It arose because after the major tanker pollution casualties the oil majors accepted that a charterer's liability and reputation do not stop at the ship's rail. OCIMF was formed in the wake of that realisation, and its Ship Inspection Report Programme (SIRE) was launched in 1993 to replace a proliferation of duplicated company inspections with one shared report.

blocks.h: 2. How the SIRE programme actually works

blocks.p: The mechanism matters, and one feature of it is routinely got wrong. SIRE is an information programme, not an approval scheme.

An accredited inspector, nominated by a submitting member company, attends the ship and completes an inspection report against the standard questionnaire. The report - together with the operator's comments, which the operator has a right to submit - is uploaded to the SIRE database. Recipient members then download it and make their own decision. OCIMF neither approves nor rejects any ship. It supplies the information; the vetting decision belongs to the individual charterer or terminal, against that company's own acceptance criteria.
The commercial value of that design is that one inspection can serve many potential charterers, which is what stops a tanker being inspected by every oil company that might fix her.

ul: VIQ - the Vessel Inspection Questionnaire. The standard question set against which the shipboard inspection is conducted. VIQ7 is the operative edition at this sitting.

HVPQ - the Harmonised Vessel Particulars Questionnaire. The standing record of the ship's particulars and equipment, maintained by the operator, which saves the inspection re-establishing what the ship is.

TMSA - Tanker Management and Self Assessment, currently in its third edition. This is the crucial complement: SIRE inspects the ship, TMSA assesses the shore-side management system, element by element, against staged levels of achievement with supporting key performance indicators. Vetting has therefore never been only about the ship.
CDI operates the parallel scheme for chemical and gas carriers; the question is confined to the oil tanker sector.

blocks.h: 4. Significance in the maritime oil trade

blocks.p: For a tanker operator, vetting is not one commercial factor among many - it is close to a licence to trade.

ul: Employment. Major charterers will not fix a tanker without an acceptable vetting position, so an adverse report can remove a ship from a whole trade without any regulatory finding against her.
Access. Terminals apply their own acceptance criteria before a ship is allowed to berth, so vetting governs where the ship can physically go.
Rate and reputation. A strong vetting and TMSA record is a marketing asset; a weak one is priced in.
Wider consequence. The same record is read by insurers, financiers and cargo interests, so its effect outlives the individual fixture.

blocks.p: The practical consequence is that the vetting standard, not the statutory minimum, sets the real operating standard in the tanker sector. A ship can be fully certificated, in class and never detained, and still be commercially unemployable.

blocks.h: 5. Continuous improvement and safety culture - and the honest criticism

blocks.p: The contribution is real, and it works through four mechanisms:

ul: Frequency and independence. A tanker is vetted far more often than she is statutorily surveyed, by inspectors with no relationship to the flag State, the society or the owner. That is a level of external scrutiny no other sector experiences.

Closed-loop correction. Observations require a response, and a serious operator routes them into the SMS as non-conformities under ISM element 9, with root-cause analysis and fleet-wide corrective action rather than a one-ship repair.

Management maturity, not just hardware. TMSA's staged self-assessment obliges a company to describe how it manages, measure itself against defined levels and show improvement over time - which addresses the causes of incidents rather than their symptoms.

Industry learning. Aggregated observations across thousands of inspections reveal trends that no single operator could see, and those trends feed back into OCIMF guidance and into the question sets themselves.

blocks.p: The honest criticism must also be made, because "discuss" invites it. Frequent inspection can produce compliance behaviour rather than safety behaviour: ships prepared for the inspection, paperwork optimised for the questionnaire, and crews drilled on the expected questions. A predictable question set is learnable, and what is learnable can be presented without being lived. There is also genuine inspection burden - vetting, PSC, class, flag, terminal and internal audits arriving on the same crew. That criticism is precisely what the developments in limb (b) are designed to answer, which is why the two limbs of this question belong together.

blocks.h: 6. SIRE 2.0 - the position at this sitting

blocks.p: The dominant development is SIRE 2.0, OCIMF's rebuilt inspection regime. Its status must be stated accurately.

SIRE 2.0 was being delivered in a four-phase roll-out rather than by a single switch-over: internal testing; a closed beta of the full end-to-end process; an unlimited beta open to all programme users as a transition period, so that submitting companies, operators and recipients could work with the system before full launch; and finally the phase in which VIQ7 is withdrawn. The unlimited beta phase was anticipated to commence towards the end of Q4 2023.

So at this examination, VIQ7 remains the operative SIRE inspection tool and SIRE 2.0 is in transition - being used, tested and prepared for, but not yet the regime. It is an emerging advancement, which is exactly the word limb (b) uses.
The changes are structural rather than cosmetic, and each one attacks a known weakness of the old model.

rows: Risk-based, bespoke questionnaire

An inspection compiler uses an algorithm to build a Compiled Vessel Inspection Questionnaire (CVIQ) for that specific ship and inspection, drawing on the HVPQ, the Pre-Inspection Questionnaire and the ship's history, with questions ranked using bowtie risk models developed with members.
One fixed questionnaire for every ship, regardless of type, trade or history.
Four question types

Core questions address significant risks and appear on every relevant inspection. Rotational questions are drawn unpredictably from a wider pool. Campaign questions are deployed across all inspections for a period in response to an incident or an industry trend. Conditional questions are triggered by the operator's own responses or the ship's history.
Predictability. A question set that can be learned can be prepared for; rotation restores genuine readiness.
Three observation tools
Every question is answered against hardware, process and human factors, and the human tool can record positive observations where performance exceeds expectation.
The binary yes-or-no snapshot, which recorded that equipment existed but not whether the system or the people worked.
Tablet-based digital inspection
Inspectors work on a tablet with camera, voice recording and location capability, producing a structured, timestamped digital record rather than a typed narrative.
Unstructured, unevidenced and slowly delivered reports.
Inspector accreditation and quality assurance
Accredited inspectors are trained to the programme, and Quality Assessors - experienced seafarers trained by OCIMF - audit inspector performance in the field.
Inconsistency between inspectors, which was the standing complaint about the old regime.

blocks.p: The human factors element is the deepest change. An inspection that formally records how work was actually performed - and can record it favourably - is asking a different question from one that asks whether a placard was posted.

blocks.h: 8. Data analytics, remote inspection, and the limits

blocks.p: Data analytics is what a structured digital report makes possible, and it works at three levels. At ship level, an operator can trend its own observations by category and by vessel instead of reading reports one at a time. At fleet and company level, the same data supports benchmarking and integrates with TMSA key performance indicators. At industry level, aggregated observations identify emerging risks - and the campaign question mechanism is the direct feedback loop, allowing the industry to interrogate a newly identified risk across every inspection within weeks rather than waiting for the next revision of a questionnaire.
Three further trends belong in the answer:

ul: Remote and hybrid inspection. Accelerated by the pandemic and now an accepted technique. The statutory world moved the same way - the 2023 HSSC Survey Guidelines, resolution A.1186(33), expressly took account of the application of remote surveys from experience gained during COVID-19 and from advanced technology.
Harmonisation and burden reduction - aligning questionnaires, sharing data between schemes and reusing standing particulars so that one crew is not asked the same questions by five organisations.
Broadening scope - cyber security, crew welfare and human element considerations entering assessment criteria alongside hardware.

blocks.p: The limits should be stated, because a discussion question rewards judgement. Analytics inherits the quality of the input, and an inconsistent observation is not improved by aggregation. The data is commercially sensitive, which constrains how widely it can be shared. Risk-based targeting can create blind spots in whatever the model treats as low risk. And a tablet does not open a crankcase: the inspector's judgement remains the instrument, and the technology's real achievement is to make that judgement consistent, evidenced and comparable rather than to replace it.

The printed split is 8 + 8, and limb (a) contains three tasks - what vetting is, why it matters commercially, and how it affects safety culture - while limb (b) contains two - the emerging trends, and specifically technology and data analytics. That is five tasks for sixteen marks, so nothing gets a leisurely paragraph.

The structural insight that lifts the answer is that the two limbs are connected. Limb (a)'s honest criticism - that a predictable inspection regime breeds preparation rather than safety - is exactly what the SIRE 2.0 developments in limb (b) were designed to fix. Ending limb (a) on that criticism and opening limb (b) by answering it turns two lists into one argument, and it is the single easiest way to look like you understand the subject rather than having memorised it.

blocks.h: The currency point - VIQ7 is still the tool at this sitting

blocks.p: This is the most easily failed question on the paper, and it fails on a date.

At January 2024, VIQ7 is still the operative SIRE inspection tool. SIRE 2.0 is in its unlimited beta transition phase, which opened towards the end of Q4 2023. SIRE 2.0 did not launch, and VIQ7 was not withdrawn, until 2 September 2024 - eight months after this sitting.

So SIRE 2.0 is the right answer to limb (b), which asks for emerging trends - but writing it as the regime in force is wrong at this date. Any material written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting will say the opposite, and copying it would be the exact error this paper is set up to catch. The safest formulation is the accurate one: "SIRE 2.0 is in phased roll-out and will replace VIQ7".

The commonest conceptual error in limb (a) is to describe OCIMF as approving or rejecting ships. It does not. SIRE is a database of inspection reports. An accredited inspector produces the report, the operator has a right to submit comments on it, and recipient member companies download it and apply their own acceptance criteria. The vetting decision belongs to the charterer or terminal, and different companies reach different decisions on the same report.
That design is also the answer to "why does SIRE exist at all?" - it replaced many duplicated company inspections with one shared report. Say that and the concept limb is complete.

blocks.h: SIRE inspects the ship; TMSA assesses the company

blocks.p: A vetting answer that mentions only shipboard inspection has described half the system. TMSA - Tanker Management and Self Assessment, in its third edition at this sitting - is the shore-side counterpart: the operator assesses its own management system element by element against staged levels of achievement, supported by key performance indicators, and the result is visible to charterers.

This matters to the safety-culture limb specifically. Hardware defects are symptoms; management systems are causes. TMSA is the part of the regime that addresses causes, and it is why vetting drives improvement ashore and not only on deck.

ul: Writing SIRE 2.0 as the current inspection regime. At this sitting it is in transition and VIQ7 is still the tool.
Saying OCIMF approves or rejects ships. It publishes reports; members decide.
Describing vetting as a statutory or regulatory requirement. It is commercial and voluntary in law - and more powerful for it.
Confusing vetting with port State control. Different question, different sanction, different body.
Omitting TMSA, and so describing only the shipboard half of the system.
Answering limb (a)'s safety-culture task with nothing but praise. "Discuss" invites the criticism too.
Answering limb (b) with a general essay about digitalisation instead of the specific SIRE 2.0 architecture.
Listing SIRE 2.0's features without saying which weakness each one attacks - the features are only interesting as answers to problems.
Quoting vetting validity periods or scoring figures. Acceptance criteria are set by each receiving company and differ between them.
"Who decides whether a ship is acceptable?" The individual charterer or terminal, against its own criteria. Not OCIMF, and not the inspector.

"Why are rotational questions a safety improvement rather than an inconvenience?" Because a fixed question set can be learned and prepared for. Unpredictability restores genuine readiness, which is the whole point.

"What is a campaign question for?" To interrogate a newly identified industry risk across every inspection immediately, rather than waiting for the questionnaire to be revised. It is the feedback loop from analytics back to the inspection.
"What are the three observation tools?" Hardware, process and human factors - and the human tool can record positive observations, which the old regime could not.

"What is the CVIQ and how is it produced?" The Compiled Vessel Inspection Questionnaire, built for that ship and that inspection by an inspection compiler drawing on the HVPQ, the Pre-Inspection Questionnaire and the ship's history.
"Does data analytics replace the inspector?" No. It makes his judgement consistent, evidenced and comparable. A tablet does not open a crankcase.

"Is a well-vetted ship necessarily a compliant ship, and vice versa?" Neither follows. A ship can be fully certificated and commercially unemployable - which is the sharpest way to state the significance of vetting.
What does SIRE stand for and when was it launched? The Ship Inspection Report Programme, launched in 1993.
Which questionnaire is in use, and what is replacing it? VIQ7, being replaced by SIRE 2.0 in a phased roll-out.
What is the difference between SIRE and TMSA? SIRE inspects the ship; TMSA assesses the shore management system.
Name the four SIRE 2.0 question types and say what each is for.
What is the HVPQ and who maintains it? The Harmonised Vessel Particulars Questionnaire, maintained by the operator.
How should a vetting observation be handled on board? As a non-conformity into the SMS under ISM element 9, with root-cause analysis and fleet-wide corrective action - not a single-ship repair.
Give one criticism of frequent vetting inspection and say how SIRE 2.0 addresses it.

blocks.p: For limb (a), four questions asked by four bodies: the flag State asks does it comply, class asks does it meet the rules, PSC asks is it substandard, and the charterer asks would I put my cargo on it. Vetting is the fourth question, and it is the only one with a commercial rather than a legal sanction.

For SIRE 2.0's question types, the four are C-R-C-C: Core always, Rotational unpredictably, Campaign when the industry needs to look at something, Conditional when this ship's own answers require it. For the observation tools, three words: hardware, process, human - the kit, the system, the people.

questions.understand_first: Vetting is the one inspection regime in shipping that has no legal force at all and yet sets the real standard. A flag State can only tell you that your ship complies; a charterer can tell you that it will not carry its cargo on your ship, and there is no appeal from that. That is why the tanker sector is inspected more often, and to a higher standard, than the law requires. The second half of the question is about what happens when that system becomes a victim of its own predictability - when everybody knows the questions, ships get ready for the inspection instead of getting ready for sea. SIRE 2.0 is the industry's answer: rotate the questions so they cannot be rehearsed, ask about the people and the process and not only the equipment, and turn every observation into data the whole industry can learn from. At this sitting that answer is being built, not yet delivered - and saying so accurately is what the question is really testing.
questions.memory_cue: Limb (a) is FOUR BODIES, FOUR QUESTIONS - flag, class, PSC, charterer - and only the last has a commercial sanction (1), then how SIRE works (2), the instruments (3), why it decides employment (4), and improvement with its honest criticism (5). Limb (b) answers that criticism: where SIRE 2.0 had got to (6), what it changes (7), and what data can and cannot do (8).

quick_revision.recall_15s: Vetting is a commercial risk assessment by a charterer, oil major or terminal deciding whether to employ a tanker - voluntary in law, decisive in practice. Flag asks does it comply, class asks does it meet the rules, PSC asks is it substandard, the charterer asks would I put my cargo on it. OCIMF's SIRE, launched 1993, is an INFORMATION programme: an accredited inspector reports, the operator may comment, recipients download and apply their own criteria - OCIMF approves nobody. VIQ7 is the operative questionnaire at this sitting; HVPQ holds the ship's particulars; TMSA 3 assesses the shore management system. Vetting drives improvement by frequency, by feeding observations into the SMS under ISM element 9, and by TMSA's staged self-assessment - but predictable inspection breeds preparation rather than safety. SIRE 2.0 is the answer and is in PHASED ROLL-OUT at this sitting, not yet in force: a bespoke CVIQ built by an inspection compiler using bowtie risk models; core, rotational, campaign and conditional questions; hardware, process and human factors observations including positive ones; tablet-based; inspectors audited by Quality Assessors. Analytics adds trending, benchmarking and campaign questions - but inherits input quality and cannot replace the inspector.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: There is no regulation here, and saying so is part of the answer. Vetting is an industry programme under OCIMF, voluntary in law and enforced commercially. The nearest regulatory contact points are ISM Code element 9, which is the route by which a vetting observation becomes a corrected non-conformity in the safety management system, and resolution A.1186(33), which shows the statutory world moving the same way on remote surveys.
quick_revision.major_trap: Writing SIRE 2.0 as the inspection regime in force. At a January 2024 sitting VIQ7 is still the operative SIRE inspection tool and SIRE 2.0 is in its unlimited beta transition phase; it did not launch, and VIQ7 was not withdrawn, until 2 September 2024 - eight months later. Material written for a 2025 or 2026 sitting says the opposite. The paired conceptual trap is saying that OCIMF approves or rejects ships: SIRE publishes reports and the recipient company makes the vetting decision.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What is a vetting inspection, and how does it differ from port State control?
retrieval_cards.answer: A commercial risk assessment by a charterer, oil major or terminal operator deciding whether to employ a particular tanker for a particular cargo and voyage. It is voluntary in law and enforced by the market. Port State control asks whether the ship is substandard and its sanction is detention; vetting asks whether the company is willing to put its cargo and reputation behind the ship, and its sanction is that the ship does not get the fixture.
retrieval_cards.why: Different question, different body, different sanction - and the commercial sanction is the more powerful of the two.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Does OCIMF approve or reject ships under SIRE?
retrieval_cards.answer: No. SIRE is an information programme. An accredited inspector produces a report, the operator has a right to submit comments, the report goes into the SIRE database, and recipient member companies download it and apply their own acceptance criteria. Different companies can and do reach different decisions on the same report.
retrieval_cards.why: The commonest conceptual error in the concept limb, and it also explains why SIRE exists - one shared report instead of many duplicated company inspections.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish SIRE from TMSA.
retrieval_cards.answer: SIRE inspects the ship, through an accredited inspector working to a questionnaire. TMSA - Tanker Management and Self Assessment, in its third edition at this sitting - assesses the shore-side management system, element by element against staged levels of achievement supported by key performance indicators. Together they cover symptom and cause.
retrieval_cards.why: An answer that mentions only shipboard inspection has described half the vetting system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: At a January 2024 sitting, which SIRE questionnaire is operative?
retrieval_cards.answer: VIQ7. SIRE 2.0 is in a four-phase roll-out and had reached its unlimited beta transition phase, which opened towards the end of Q4 2023, but it did not launch and VIQ7 was not withdrawn until 2 September 2024. SIRE 2.0 is therefore correctly described as the emerging regime, not the regime in force.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the single date on which the question is most easily failed, and later material states the opposite.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the four SIRE 2.0 question types and what each is for.
retrieval_cards.answer: Core - questions addressing significant risks, appearing on every relevant inspection. Rotational - drawn unpredictably from a wider pool so the inspection cannot be rehearsed. Campaign - deployed across all inspections for a period in response to an incident or industry trend. Conditional - triggered by the operator's own responses or by the ship's history.
retrieval_cards.why: Rotational and campaign questions are the two that answer the criticisms in limb (a), which is what connects the two limbs.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the three SIRE 2.0 observation tools, and why do they matter?
retrieval_cards.answer: Hardware, process and human factors. Every question is answered against all three, and the human tool can record positive observations where performance exceeds expectation. They replace a binary yes-or-no snapshot which recorded that equipment existed but not whether the system or the people worked.
retrieval_cards.why: The human factors element is the deepest change in SIRE 2.0 and the one that most affects safety culture.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How is a SIRE 2.0 inspection questionnaire produced?
retrieval_cards.answer: An inspection compiler uses an algorithm to build a bespoke Compiled Vessel Inspection Questionnaire for that ship and that inspection, drawing on the Harmonised Vessel Particulars Questionnaire, the Pre-Inspection Questionnaire and the ship's history, with questions ranked using bowtie risk assessment models developed with OCIMF members.
retrieval_cards.why: It is what makes the regime risk-based rather than one fixed questionnaire for every ship.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the honest criticism of frequent vetting inspection.
retrieval_cards.answer: It can produce compliance behaviour rather than safety behaviour - ships prepared for the inspection, paperwork optimised for the questionnaire, crews drilled on the expected questions. A predictable question set is learnable, and what is learnable can be presented without being lived. There is also real inspection burden, with vetting, PSC, class, flag, terminal and internal audits falling on the same crew.
retrieval_cards.why: "Discuss" invites the criticism, and stating it is what sets up limb (b) as the answer to it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: How should a vetting observation be handled on board?
retrieval_cards.answer: As a non-conformity routed into the safety management system under ISM Code element 9, with the possible cause recorded, root-cause analysis carried out and corrective action applied across the fleet - not as a single-ship repair closed out before the next inspection.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the mechanism by which vetting actually produces continuous improvement rather than cosmetic compliance.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What are the limits of data analytics in vetting?
retrieval_cards.answer: Analytics inherits the quality of its input, and an inconsistent observation is not improved by aggregation. The data is commercially sensitive, which constrains sharing. Risk-based targeting can create blind spots wherever the model treats something as low risk. And the inspector's judgement remains the instrument - the technology makes it consistent, evidenced and comparable rather than replacing it.
retrieval_cards.why: A discussion question rewards judgement, and naming the limits is what distinguishes discussion from description.

blocks.h: 1. What FTA is, and how it differs from the alternatives

blocks.p: Fault Tree Analysis is a deductive, top-down technique. It begins with one precisely defined undesired event - the top event - and works backwards through the immediate, necessary and sufficient causes of that event, level by level, until it reaches events which need no further development. The logic connecting the levels is Boolean, expressed through gates.
The direction of travel is what distinguishes it, and naming the alternatives earns the mark:

ul: FTA - deductive, from one failure backwards to its many causes. Answers: how can this happen?
FMEA - inductive, from each component forwards to its effects. Answers: what happens if this fails? It is exhaustive on components but poor at combinations.
Event Tree Analysis - inductive, from an initiating event forwards through the success or failure of each barrier, to the range of outcomes.
HAZOP - guideword-driven, applied to a process or design rather than to a defined failure.

blocks.p: FTA is the right tool when there is one failure you care about very much and you need to know every way it can arise - a blackout, loss of steering, failure of the emergency fire pump to start on demand. It is the wrong tool for a general survey of everything that could go wrong; FMEA does that better.

The top event, and every intermediate event - a fault developed further by a gate below it.
