A basic event - a primary failure requiring no further development. The resolution limit of the tree.
Diamond
An undeveloped event - one which could be developed but is not, for want of information or because it is outside the scope.
House
A house or external event - something normally expected to occur, or a boundary condition switched on or off to test the tree.
Triangle
Transfer in and out - a branch continued on another sheet, which is how a large tree stays readable.
AND gate
The output occurs only if ALL inputs occur. An AND gate is the signature of redundancy.
OR gate
The output occurs if ANY input occurs. An OR gate is the signature of a series dependency - and of a single-point failure.

blocks.p: An INHIBIT gate, drawn as a hexagon with a conditioning event alongside, passes its input only when a stated condition holds - useful where a failure only matters in a particular operating mode.

ol: Define the top event precisely, with its boundary conditions - which system, which operating mode, what counts as failure. "Engine trouble" is not a top event; "main engine fails to start on demand from the bridge, at sea, in remote control" is.
Identify the immediate, necessary and sufficient causes of that event - the level directly beneath it, and no lower. Skipping a level is the commonest drafting error and it hides gates.
Choose the gate - OR if any one cause alone produces the event, AND if all are required together.
Develop each intermediate event the same way, one level at a time.

Stop at the resolution limit - a component failure, a human error or an external event that you will not or cannot analyse further. Draw it as a basic event, or as a diamond if it is merely undeveloped.
Evaluate - qualitatively by minimal cut sets, and quantitatively only if credible failure data exists.

blocks.h: 4. What the finished tree is used for

blocks.p: A cut set is any combination of basic events which together cause the top event. A minimal cut set is one from which no event can be removed without the combination ceasing to cause the top event. The order of a cut set is the number of basic events in it, and the order is the whole point:

ul: an order-1 minimal cut set is a single-point failure - one basic event, on its own, defeats the system. Finding these is the primary value of the technique;
a low-order cut set concentrates risk; a high-order one implies real redundancy;
a basic event appearing in many cut sets is a common-cause candidate, and common cause is what makes nominal redundancy illusory - two pumps on one switchboard, two systems in one flooded space.

blocks.p: On board, the outputs are practical. The single-point failures identify critical equipment - which is the judgement ISM Code element 10.3 requires, and it drives the specific reliability measures and the regular testing of stand-by arrangements not in continuous use that the same paragraph demands. The tree also supports incident investigation under element 9, redundancy decisions at design and retrofit, and the risk analysis step of a Formal Safety Assessment. Quantification is optional and depends on failure data the ship does not usually hold; the qualitative tree is valuable without it.

blocks.h: (b) A fault tree for the printed top event

blocks.p: The printed question defines two different failures and this must be dealt with, not ignored. It names the top event "Engine Starting Failure" and then glosses it as "the engine speed goes down and finally stops" - which is a running engine losing speed and stopping, not a failure to start.

The safe response, and the one taken here, is to state the ambiguity in one line and develop both under a single top event: MAIN ENGINE UNAVAILABLE TO PROPEL - fails to start on demand, or having started, loses speed and stops. The two share their fuel, control and support branches, so the tree is not doubled by covering both. Boundary conditions: main propulsion engine, at sea, bridge or engine-room control, no external damage assumed.
The top gate is an OR - any one branch alone produces the top event.

blocks.h: 6. Branch A - starting air and admission

blocks.p: ENGINE FAILS TO TURN ON AIR — via OR:

ul: Insufficient starting air pressure — OR: air compressors fail to deliver (compressor mechanical failure; motor or starter failure; power loss); receiver isolated or drained; system leakage; non-return valve failure; repeated failed start attempts exhausting the receivers.
Main starting air valve does not open — OR: control air pressure low; solenoid or pilot valve failure; valve seized; blocked control air line.
Starting air distributor fault — OR: distributor timing incorrect; pilot air passage blocked; distributor seized.
Cylinder starting air valve fails to open — OR: valve seized; spring failure; air supply to that valve blocked.

Interlock not satisfied — OR: turning gear engaged; main starting valve in shut or blocked position; control air low; auxiliary blower not running where required; control lever not in the correct position.
Engine turns but does not fire — develops into Branch B (transfer).

blocks.p: Note that most of these sit under OR gates - each is a single-point failure. Where two compressors and two receivers are fitted, that sub-branch becomes an AND gate and the failure order rises. That contrast is exactly what the tree is drawn to reveal.
NO OR INSUFFICIENT COMBUSTION — via OR:

ul: Fuel not reaching the injection pumps — OR: service tank empty or valve shut; supply or booster pump failure (mechanical, or motor and power loss); filters blocked; air locked in the system; water in the fuel; fuel too viscous through heater or trace-heating failure; wax at low temperature on a distillate.

Fuel not injected — OR: injection pump defect or plunger seizure; injector nozzle blocked or lifting pressure incorrect; high-pressure pipe fracture; on an electronically controlled engine, servo or control oil pressure low, or a control system fault.

Fuel rack at zero — OR: governor failure or hunting; actuator or linkage failure; a shutdown or trip signal commanding zero fuel; emergency stop operated locally or from the bridge; remote control system fault; fuel limiter acting.
Combustion conditions inadequate — OR: insufficient scavenge air; low compression from leaking piston rings, exhaust or starting air valves; charge air cooler flooded or fouled.

blocks.h: 8. Branch C - trips, load and support systems

blocks.p: This is the branch the printed gloss - speed going down and the engine stopping - actually describes.
ENGINE SHUTS DOWN OR IS SLOWED WHILE RUNNING — via OR:

ul: Automatic safety shutdown or slowdown operates — OR: lubricating oil low pressure; jacket cooling water high temperature or low pressure; piston cooling failure; thrust bearing high temperature; oil mist detector high; overspeed; camshaft or servo oil low pressure; and, on each of these, the possibility of a spurious trip from a faulty sensor or transmitter rather than a real condition.

Support system lost — OR: blackout, taking lubricating oil, cooling water and fuel supply pumps with it; control air failure; sea water cooling failure through a blocked suction, a failed pump or a fouled cooler.
Excessive load — OR: heavy running propeller from a fouled hull or a damaged blade; severe weather; shallow water; ice.
Turbocharger failure or surging, reducing scavenge air and torque - which then reappears in Branch B under inadequate combustion conditions.
Mechanical distress — OR: bearing wipe or seizure; piston or liner seizure; broken piston rod or coupling.
Fuel supply interrupted while running - transfer to Branch B.

blocks.p: Human and organisational events sit across all three branches and belong in the tree rather than in a footnote: indicator cocks left open, wrong control station selected, turning gear left engaged, incorrect starting procedure, tanks not changed over or topped up, a trip not reset, maintenance not carried out.
The value is in what the structure shows once it is drawn.

ul: The tree is dominated by OR gates, which means the top event has many order-1 minimal cut sets - many single-point failures. That is the correct and sobering finding for a single-screw ship.

Where the design provides genuine redundancy the gate becomes AND - two air compressors, two receivers, duplicated lubricating oil pumps, two generators on the board - and the cut set order rises accordingly. Comparing the OR-heavy branches with the AND branches is precisely how a fault tree justifies a redundancy decision.

Common cause is the trap. Two lubricating oil pumps fed from one switchboard, or two air receivers charged by compressors on one starter panel, are drawn as an AND gate but behave as an OR. A basic event appearing in many cut sets should be examined for exactly this.

Control and instrumentation appear more often than machinery. A spurious trip stops the engine as effectively as a real fault, which is why trip testing, sensor calibration and override philosophy carry so much weight.

The output is a work list. Every order-1 cut set is a candidate for critical equipment under ISM 10.3, and the stand-by arrangements it identifies are exactly the ones that paragraph requires to be regularly tested.

blocks.p: In the examination, draw this with the standard symbols - rectangles for the top and intermediate events, circles for basic events, and the AND and OR gates clearly marked - and use transfer triangles for the fuel branch rather than drawing it twice.

The printed split is 8 + 8, and the two limbs need completely different treatment. Limb (a) is theory and is best answered with a symbol table and a numbered method - it is bookwork and should be written quickly and precisely. Limb (b) is a drawing, and eight marks for a drawing means the examiner is counting branches, gates and levels.

The single most valuable habit in limb (b) is to develop breadth before depth. Get the three or four main branches down under the top gate first, then fill each one. A tree with three well-developed branches scores far better than one branch analysed to exhaustion while the others are missing - and if time runs out, a broad shallow tree still shows you understand the method.

blocks.h: The printed top event contradicts itself - say so

blocks.p: This is the discriminating feature of the question and most candidates will not notice it. The examiner names the top event "Engine Starting Failure" and then defines it as "the engine speed goes down and finally stops". Those are two different failures: one is an engine that will not start, the other is a running engine that stops.

Do not choose one and hope. Do not silently correct the examiner. State the ambiguity in a single line and develop both under one top event - main engine unavailable to propel: fails to start, or having started, loses speed and stops. The two failures share their fuel, control and support-system branches, so covering both costs far less than it looks, and it demonstrates exactly the precision about top-event definition that limb (a) says is the first step of the method. That is a mark for reading the question.

blocks.h: AND and OR are the whole of the analysis

blocks.p: Everything a fault tree tells you comes out of which gate you drew. OR means any one input alone causes the output - a series dependency, and a single-point failure. AND means all inputs are required - which is what redundancy looks like on paper.

So an engine tree that is almost entirely OR gates is not a badly drawn tree; it is a true statement about a single-screw ship. The interesting places are the few AND gates - two compressors, two receivers, duplicated pumps - and the places where an AND gate is a lie because of common cause. Two lubricating oil pumps on one switchboard are drawn as AND and behave as OR. Say that in an oral and the examiner will know you have used the technique rather than read about it.

blocks.h: Cut sets, and why order matters

blocks.p: A cut set is any set of basic events that together cause the top event; a minimal cut set is one you cannot remove anything from. The order is how many events it contains.

Order 1 is a single-point failure. Finding those is the main reason to draw the tree at all, and on board it feeds straight into the critical equipment list required by ISM element 10.3 - which is also why that paragraph insists on regular testing of stand-by arrangements not in continuous use. A basic event that turns up in many cut sets is a common-cause suspect. Connect the tree to ISM 10.3 explicitly: it converts an academic answer into a management-level one.

ul: Not noticing that the printed top event describes two different failures.
Defining the top event loosely. "Engine problem" cannot be developed; a precise event with boundary conditions can.
Skipping levels - jumping from the top event straight to basic events. It hides the gates, which are the analysis.
Drawing the tree with no gates at all, as a mind map of causes. Without AND and OR it is not a fault tree.
Using AND where OR is meant. If either cause alone stops the engine, it is OR.
Analysing one branch to exhaustion and never drawing the others. Breadth first.
Forgetting human and organisational events - turning gear engaged, indicator cocks open, wrong control station, trip not reset.
Forgetting spurious trips. A faulty sensor stops the engine exactly as effectively as a real low oil pressure.
Confusing FTA with FMEA. FTA works backwards from one failure; FMEA works forwards from every component.
Quoting failure probabilities. Quantitative FTA needs plant-specific data no candidate holds.
"Is FTA inductive or deductive?" Deductive - top-down, from one defined failure backwards to its causes. FMEA and event tree analysis are inductive.

"What does a diamond mean, and how does it differ from a circle?" A circle is a basic event, developed no further because it needs no further development. A diamond is an undeveloped event - it could be developed but is not, for want of data or because it lies outside the scope.
"What is a minimal cut set of order one?" A single-point failure. One basic event alone causes the top event.

"You have two lubricating oil pumps and drew an AND gate. Is the engine safe?" Only if the redundancy is real. If both pumps take power from the same switchboard, the common cause defeats the AND gate.
"Your engine stopped and every parameter was normal." Suspect a spurious trip - a faulty sensor or transmitter - or a control system fault. That branch belongs in the tree.

"What would you do with the completed tree on board?" Extract the single-point failures, use them to build or challenge the critical equipment list under ISM 10.3, and set the testing regime for stand-by arrangements accordingly.
"When would you use FMEA instead?" When surveying a whole system for the effects of every component failure, rather than investigating one specific failure you already care about.

blocks.p: For the method, six steps in one line: DEFINE, IMMEDIATE CAUSES, GATE, DEVELOP, STOP, EVALUATE. For the gates, two words: OR is ANY, AND is ALL - and AND means redundancy.

For the engine tree, the three branches are AIR, FUEL, STOP. Air - can it be turned? Fuel - can it fire? Stop - is something shutting it down or holding it back? Every cause you can think of belongs in one of those three, and human error runs across all three.
Within the shutdown branch, the trips run in the order you would check them: oil, water, temperature, mist, speed.

ul: ISM Code element 10.3 - identify equipment and technical systems the sudden operational failure of which may result in hazardous situations; provide specific measures to promote reliability, including regular testing of stand-by arrangements and equipment not in continuous use. This is the shipboard use of a fault tree and the single regulatory anchor of the question.
ISM Code element 9 - reports and analysis of non-conformities, accidents and hazardous occurrences; the investigative context for drawing a tree after an event.
IMO Formal Safety Assessment - fault trees are used within its risk analysis step. Named as context only.

The FTA method itself, the symbol set, gate semantics and minimal cut sets are standard reliability engineering. No IMO instrument prescribes them, and the answer declares that rather than inventing an authority - see PASTPAPER_PRODUCTION_PROTOCOL section 2.1.

blocks.h: Uncertainty, the printed anomaly and the absence of numbers

blocks.p: The printed top event is internally inconsistent and has been preserved exactly as printed. "Engine Starting Failure" and "the engine speed goes down and finally stops" describe two different failures. The source has not been corrected into what the examiner probably meant; the anomaly is recorded, and the answer resolves it by developing both readings under one top event - which is also the best examination-room response.

No failure rate, probability or MTBF appears anywhere. Quantitative FTA requires plant-specific failure data which no candidate holds and which would differ for every installation. The answer explains the qualitative evaluation - which is what the question asks for - and states what quantification would require rather than inventing a number to look rigorous.

The tree given is a worked example, not a complete analysis of any particular engine. Trips, interlocks and control architecture differ between makers, and between camshaft-controlled and electronically controlled engines. The answer says so rather than presenting one tree as universal. The dominant provenance class of this question is engineering judgement over standard reliability practice, and it is declared rather than disguised.

questions.understand_first: A fault tree is a way of being systematic about the question every engineer asks after a breakdown: how could this possibly have happened? Instead of listing everything that might go wrong, you start with the one failure you cannot tolerate and work backwards, one honest level at a time, asking what would have to be true immediately beneath. The gates are the whole analysis: OR means any one of these alone does it, AND means they all have to happen together - which is what redundancy looks like when you draw it. Once the tree is finished you look for the places where a single circle, on its own, reaches the top. Those are your critical items, and on a ship that list is not academic: it is exactly what the ISM Code obliges the Company to identify and to keep testing. The second half of this question also hides a small trap - the examiner's own words describe two different failures, and noticing that is itself the first step of the method.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Define Fault Tree Analysis and state its direction of reasoning.
retrieval_cards.answer: A deductive, top-down technique which begins with one precisely defined undesired top event and works backwards through the immediate, necessary and sufficient causes, level by level, to basic events needing no further development. The levels are connected by Boolean gates.
retrieval_cards.why: Deductive and top-down is the phrase that distinguishes it from every other technique in the syllabus.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Distinguish FTA, FMEA and event tree analysis.
retrieval_cards.answer: FTA is deductive - from one failure backwards to its many causes, asking how can this happen. FMEA is inductive - from each component forwards to its effects, asking what happens if this fails; it is exhaustive on components but poor at combinations. Event tree analysis is inductive - from an initiating event forwards through the success or failure of each barrier to the range of outcomes.
retrieval_cards.why: One mark for each direction of reasoning, and it is the fastest way to show the techniques are understood rather than listed.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the fault tree symbols and what each means.
retrieval_cards.answer: Rectangle - the top event and every intermediate event developed by a gate below it. Circle - a basic event, the resolution limit. Diamond - an undeveloped event, which could be developed but is not. House - an external event or boundary condition. Triangle - transfer in and out, continuing a branch elsewhere. Plus the AND and OR gates, and the INHIBIT gate with its conditioning event.
retrieval_cards.why: Circle versus diamond is the distinction most often confused, and it is easy marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What does an AND gate tell you about the design, and when does it lie?
retrieval_cards.answer: That all inputs must occur together for the output to occur - which is what genuine redundancy looks like on paper. It lies when the redundant items share a common cause: two lubricating oil pumps fed from the same switchboard, or two systems in the same compartment, are drawn as AND but behave as OR.
retrieval_cards.why: Common-cause failure is the single most valuable insight the technique produces.

retrieval_cards.answer: A cut set is any combination of basic events which together cause the top event; a minimal cut set is one from which no event can be removed without the combination ceasing to cause it. The order is the number of basic events in it. An order-1 minimal cut set is a single-point failure - one event alone defeats the system.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The engine stopped and every parameter read normal. Where does that sit in the tree?
retrieval_cards.answer: Under the shutdown branch, as a spurious trip - a faulty sensor, transmitter or control system fault commanding a shutdown when no real condition existed. A spurious trip stops the engine exactly as effectively as a genuine low oil pressure, which is why instrumentation appears in the tree more often than machinery does.
retrieval_cards.why: Candidates draw only real faults; the control system is where a surprising share of the cut sets actually live.

The discriminating expectations are that the candidate notices the contradiction in the printed top event, includes human and organisational events, and includes spurious trips rather than only genuine faults.

blocks.h: 1. The Code, and what made a recommendatory text mandatory

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) is the annex to resolution A.1070(28), adopted by the Assembly on 4 December 2013. Its operative paragraph 3 revoked resolution A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011, which had underpinned the earlier voluntary audit scheme.

The Code reads throughout in the language of recommendation - it says what a State "should" do - and candidates are often unable to explain why such a text binds anyone. The answer is that the Code was never redrafted into obligation language; the conventions were amended to require its use. The chain is recited in the preamble to A.1187(33):

ul: A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) amended Load Lines 1966, Tonnage 1969 and COLREG 1972;
MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) amended SOLAS 1974, STCW 1978, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol;
MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) amended MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol.

blocks.p: That chain is what makes the Code the standard against which a Member State is audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme. The Code has four parts - Part 1 Common Areas, Part 2 Flag States, Part 3 Coastal States, Part 4 Port States - and each of Parts 2, 3 and 4 ends with an Evaluation and review section. Limb (b) is simply the flag State's evaluation section opened up.

Paragraph 1 states it in a single sentence: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization. The second half is dropped by most candidates and it is half the sentence - the Code is an assistance instrument, written because the Organization accepted that some States face real difficulty in complying fully.

Paragraph 2 qualifies it immediately. States will view the Code according to their own circumstances and should be bound only for the implementation of those instruments to which they are Contracting Governments or Parties; by virtue of geography and circumstance some States act principally as flag States, others as coastal or port States. The Code is therefore not a uniform checklist applied identically everywhere.

Two general duties frame everything that follows. Paragraph 4 makes States responsible for promulgating laws and regulations and taking all other steps necessary to give those instruments full and complete effect. Paragraph 5 requires that, in acting against pollution, a State must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, nor transform one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: 3. The strategy recommended to the State

blocks.p: Paragraph 3 answers the second half of limb (a). To meet the objective a State is recommended to:

ol: develop an overall strategy to ensure that its international obligations and responsibilities as a flag, port and coastal State are met (3.1);
establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy ensures effective implementation and enforcement of the relevant international mandatory instruments (3.2); and
continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve overall organizational performance and capability as a flag, port and coastal State (3.3).

blocks.p: Read together those three are a develop - monitor - review cycle, not a document written once and filed. Paragraph 9 completes it: the State should communicate its strategy, including information on its national legislation, to all concerned.

Paragraph 7 then says what the legislation and administrative procedures must actually address - nine areas: jurisdiction; organization and authority; legislation, rules and regulations; promulgation of the applicable mandatory instruments; enforcement arrangements; control, survey, inspection, audit, verification, approval and certification functions; the selection, recognition, authorization, empowerment and monitoring of recognized organizations and nominated surveyors; investigations required to be reported to the Organization; and reporting to the Organization and other Administrations. Paragraph 8 adds the three initial actions a Government must be capable of when a new or amended instrument enters into force: the ability to promulgate laws giving effective jurisdiction and control, a legal basis for enforcement including investigative and penal processes, and sufficient personnel with maritime expertise.

blocks.h: 4. Which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: This limb has two correct answers and they are not the same, which is where the marks are usually lost.

First, the Code's own scope. Paragraph 6 says the Code addresses those aspects necessary to give full and complete effect to the applicable international instruments pertaining to six subject areas: safety of life at sea; prevention of pollution from ships; standards of training, certification and watchkeeping for seafarers; load lines; tonnage measurement of ships; and regulations for preventing collisions at sea.

Note what is absent. Maritime security is not one of the six. The resolution's preamble speaks of safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the operative scope at paragraph 6 does not extend to the ISPS Code or SOLAS chapter XI-2.

Second, the treaty instruments under which use of the Code is mandatory, which therefore define the audit scope. These are listed in resolution A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code, adopted on 6 December 2023 - one month before this examination. They are SOLAS 1974 with its 1978 and 1988 Protocols; MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; Tonnage 1969; and COLREG 1972.

Two features of A.1187(33) are worth carrying into the answer. Its operative paragraph 4 revoked A.1157(32), the 2021 list, so material citing the 2021 list is superseded at this sitting. And its annex is arranged in seven annexes - obligations of Contracting Governments and Parties; specific flag, coastal and port State obligations; instruments made mandatory under IMO conventions; a summary of amendments; and, as Annex 7, amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024. At this sitting that last annex is a forward-looking list - a clean illustration that adopted is not the same as in force.

blocks.h: 5. Key performance indicators for flag State evaluation

blocks.p: Paragraph 42 requires a flag State to evaluate its performance on a periodic basis with respect to the administrative processes, procedures and resources needed to meet its obligations. Paragraph 43 then lists the measures, inter alia:

ul: port State control detention rates;
flag State inspection results;
casualty statistics;
communication and information processes;
annual loss statistics, excluding constructive total losses (CTLs); and
such other performance indicators as may be appropriate.

blocks.p: Quoting the stated purpose earns the mark, because it shows the paragraph has been read rather than remembered: the indicators exist in order to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet its flag State obligations. They are for the State's own self-evaluation, not a return submitted to IMO.

Paragraph 44 then recommends ten areas for regular review: fleet loss and accident ratios to identify trends over selected periods; the number of verified cases of detained ships in relation to the size of the fleet; verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by holders of certificates or endorsements issued under its authority; responses to port State deficiency reports or interventions; investigations into very serious and serious casualties and the lessons learned; technical and other resources committed; results of inspections, surveys and controls of ships in the fleet; investigation of occupational accidents; the number of incidents and violations under the applicable pollution prevention regulations; and the number of suspensions or withdrawals of certificates, endorsements or approvals.
Part 2 is the longest part of the Code, paragraphs 15 to 44, and its shape is implementation - delegation - enforcement - surveyors - investigations - review.

ul: Implementation (15 to 17). Issue national legislation and guidance implementing the safety and pollution conventions, and assign responsibility for keeping it updated. Paragraph 16 requires a safety and environmental protection programme with five minimum elements, of which the load-bearing one is 16.2 - compliance verified by an audit and inspection programme independent of any body issuing the certificates. Paragraph 17 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned, on the Principles of Safe Manning.

Delegation (18 to 21). A flag State authorising a recognized organization must determine that it has adequate technical, managerial and research capability; base the authorisation on a formal written agreement; issue specific instructions for a ship found unfit to proceed to sea; supply its national law and interpretations; and require records to be kept. Paragraph 20 requires an oversight programme with supplementary surveys and competent supervising staff.

Enforcement (22 to 27). Prohibit a ship from sailing until it complies; inspect periodically to verify that the actual condition of ship and crew matches the certificates; verify seafarer familiarity and the crew's ability to coordinate in an emergency; provide penalties of adequate severity; and institute proceedings after investigation irrespective of where the violation occurred. Paragraphs 26 and 27 permit certification only after determining that all applicable requirements are met.

Surveyors and investigations (28 to 41). Surveyors qualified against a defined standard, worked under a documented qualification system and issued an identification document. Marine safety investigations by impartial and objective investigators, taking account of the Casualty Investigation Code, with the report forwarded to the Organization together with the flag State's observations.

blocks.h: 7. Coastal State and port State responsibilities

blocks.p: Parts 3 and 4 open on the same principle, at paragraphs 45 and 52: coastal and port States have rights as well as obligations, and when they exercise those rights they incur additional obligations. Both must implement policy through national legislation and guidance, and ensure their procedures deliver consistent implementation and verification.

Coastal State (Part 3). Paragraph 48 lists the rights, obligations and responsibilities, inter alia: radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation - eight service areas. Note their character: they are services to shipping, not controls over ships. Paragraph 50 requires a control and monitoring programme allocating statistical data for trend analysis, mechanisms for timely response to pollution incidents in its waters, and cooperation with flag and port States in casualty investigations.

Port State (Part 4). Paragraph 53 records that the port State role derives from a combination of treaties, conventions, national laws and in some cases bilateral and multilateral agreements. Paragraph 56 gives three obligations: provision of appropriate reception facilities or the capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers. Paragraph 59 carries the no more favourable treatment principle - the conditions of the instruments are imposed on ships of non-parties as well as parties. Paragraphs 60 and 61 require a PSC programme consistent with the relevant Assembly resolution - at this sitting that is resolution A.1185(33), the Procedures for Port State Control, 2023, adopted 6 December 2023 and revoking A.1155(32) - carried out only by authorized and qualified port State control officers. Paragraph 62 requires those officers to be free from commercial, financial and other pressures, to hold no commercial interest in the port, the ships inspected, repair facilities or support services, and not to be employed by or work on behalf of recognized organizations or classification societies.

Both parts close as Part 2 does: paragraphs 51 and 63 require the coastal State and the port State to periodically evaluate their own performance. That symmetry - implement, enforce, evaluate - is the single most useful thing to carry into the examination hall, because it lets you structure all three States from one remembered shape.

The printed marks are 6 + 4 + 6, and limb (a) hides four tasks inside its six: what this Code is, its objective, its recommended strategy, and which instruments it covers. Splitting limb (a) across route steps 2, 3 and 4, with the framing in step 1, is what stops the six marks being spent on a single paragraph about the objective.

Limb (b) is only four marks but has a precise source - paragraphs 43 and 44 - so a candidate who names the indicators in the Code's own words banks those marks quickly and buys time for limb (c). Limb (c) covers three States in six marks, roughly two each, and the Code makes that tractable because Parts 2, 3 and 4 share one skeleton: implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. Answer all three on that skeleton and the examiner sees structure rather than a list.

blocks.h: The mandatory-application chain, and why it matters

blocks.p: Candidates routinely assert that "the III Code is mandatory" without being able to say why a text written entirely in "should" binds anybody. The answer is that the Code was never redrafted into obligation language; the conventions were amended to require its use. That is why it still reads as recommendation throughout.

Being able to give the chain in one sentence - A.1083, A.1084 and A.1085(28) for Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG; MSC.366, MSC.373, MSC.374 and MSC.375(93) for SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; MEPC.246 and MEPC.247(66) for MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol - distinguishes a candidate who has opened the instrument from one who has read about it. The chain is recited in the preamble to A.1187(33), so it is easy to check and easy to learn.

blocks.h: The obligations list is ONE MONTH old at this sitting

blocks.p: This is the currency point of the question and it is unusually sharp here. Resolution A.1187(33) was adopted on 6 December 2023 - one month before this examination - and its operative paragraph 4 revoked A.1157(32), the 2021 list. Any material citing the 2021 list is superseded at this sitting.

There is a second, better point available. A.1187(33)'s annex states that it takes account of amendments which have, or are expected to have, entered into force by or on 1 July 2024, and its Annex 7 is headed amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024. At a January 2024 sitting that annex is looking forward - it lists things that have not happened yet. If you want one sentence that proves you understand the difference between adopted and in force, that is it.
The printed words are "Which all IMO instruments covered in the code". Two different things are being asked at once and the safe answer gives both.

The Code's scope at paragraph 6 is expressed as six subject areas and does not name a single convention: safety of life at sea; prevention of pollution from ships; training, certification and watchkeeping; load lines; tonnage measurement; and preventing collisions at sea. The instruments under which the Code is mandatory are a different list entirely - the SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG family with their Protocols, set out in A.1187(33). Give both, and say why they differ.

A count is risky. The audit scope is commonly summarised as nine mandatory instruments - SOLAS 1974, SOLAS PROT 1988, MARPOL, MARPOL PROT 1997, STCW 1978, LL 1966, LL PROT 1988, TONNAGE 1969 and COLREG 1972 - but A.1187(33) also carries a SOLAS PROT 1978 column, which is why ten also circulates, and neither resolution states a number anywhere. List them; do not lead with a count. If pressed, say "the SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG instruments together with their Protocols, commonly summarised as nine".

The absence of maritime security from paragraph 6 is a genuine examinable point, not a drafting slip: the preamble uses the phrase "safety, security and protection of the marine environment" while the operative scope does not extend to security instruments.

ul: Writing a general essay on flag State duties under UNCLOS article 94. That is a different question. The examiner has named a specific Code and wants its paragraphs.
Answering "which instruments" with the six subject areas only, or with the convention list only. Give both and explain why they differ.
Confusing the III Code with the ISM Code. The III Code binds States; the ISM Code binds companies and ships.
Treating the performance indicators as a return made to IMO. They are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation under paragraph 42.
Giving the coastal State a control-and-inspection role. Paragraph 48 is a list of services - SAR, hydrography, VTS, aids to navigation.
Citing A.1054(27) as current. It was revoked by A.1070(28).
Citing the 2021 obligations list, A.1157(32). It was revoked by A.1187(33) one month before this sitting.
Leading with a count of mandatory instruments. Neither resolution states one.
Spending half the answer on limb (c) because it is familiar. It is worth six marks, the same as limb (a).
Six subject areas versus the instrument list. The single most likely place to lose marks on this question.
"Should" throughout the Code. Asked whether the Code is mandatory, the answer is that its use is mandatory under the amended conventions while the text remains recommendatory in form.
Excluding constructive total losses. Paragraph 43 says annual loss statistics excluding CTLs. Reproducing that qualifier shows the source has been read.

Two independence requirements, and do not merge them. The flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of the body issuing the certificates (16.2); port State control officers must be free of commercial interest and must not work for recognized organizations or classification societies (62). Different Parts, different purposes.
"Which PSC procedures apply?" At this sitting, A.1185(33), the Procedures for Port State Control 2023, adopted 6 December 2023 and revoking A.1155(32).
"Name the three port State obligations." Reception facilities, port State control, and a register of fuel oil suppliers. The register is the one candidates forget.
"What does Annex 7 of A.1187(33) contain, and why is that interesting today?" Amendments expected to enter into force between 1 January and 1 July 2024 - which at this sitting have not yet done so.
Is the III Code mandatory, and how? Use the amendment chain.
What is IMSAS and what does it audit against? The Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligations list.

Your flag State has a rising detention rate. What does the Code expect it to do? Paragraphs 43 and 44 - treat it as a performance indicator, review detentions against fleet size and responses to PSC deficiency reports, and test whether staffing and resources are adequate.
What must a flag State do before authorising a class society? Paragraph 18 - capability, a formal written agreement, specific instructions for unfit ships, national law and interpretations, records.
Name the eight coastal State service areas.

Which State investigates a casualty, and who receives the report? The flag State provides qualified investigators irrespective of where the casualty occurred; the report goes to the Organization with the flag State's observations.
Which resolution carries the current obligations list, and what did it revoke?

blocks.p: Two shapes carry the whole question. The Code's shape is common areas, then flag, then coastal, then port. The shape inside each State part is implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. blocks.p: The answer deliberately does not lead with a number of instruments. A.1070(28) states six subject areas and no instrument count; A.1187(33) lists obligations by instrument without totalling them. The figure of nine is a widely used summary and is offered as such, not as a quotation. A candidate who writes "nine" will not be marked wrong; a candidate who lists them cannot be.

Two different verification classes are used in this answer and they are distinguished rather than blurred. Resolution A.1187(33) was read directly from the local corpus for this question - its preamble, its four operative paragraphs, its annex currency statement and its seven-annex structure - so the mandatory-application chain, the revocation of A.1157(32) and the Annex 7 point are primary verified. Currency. A.1070(28) is unamended between its adoption in 2013 and this sitting. A.1187(33) was adopted one month before this sitting and is the current list. questions.understand_first: The examiner has named one instrument and is checking whether you have opened it. Every mark on this question is inside resolution A.1070(28), and the Code is short - sixty-three paragraphs in four parts. Better still, it is organised exactly the way the question is: common material first, then flag, coastal and port States in that order, each part ending in an evaluation and review section. Limb (b) IS that evaluation section of the flag State part. So if you can hold the Code's own structure you can rebuild the whole answer from it. The one place the question is sharper than the Code is "which all IMO instruments" - because the Code answers that with six SUBJECT AREAS, while the instruments it is mandatory under are a different list entirely. And at this particular sitting there is a bonus: the obligations list was adopted one month ago, and its final annex is still looking forward at things that have not entered into force yet.
questions.memory_cue: The Code's four parts give the answer its spine - COMMON, FLAG, COASTAL, PORT. Walk it as WHAT-WHY-HOW-WHICH-MEASURE-WHO: WHAT the Code is and what binds it (1), WHY it exists (2), HOW a State meets it (3), WHICH instruments it reaches (4), how performance is MEASURED (5), and WHO does what - flag (6), then coastal and port (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: The III Code is the annex to A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013, which revoked A.1054(27). It is recommendatory in wording but mandatory in use, because SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG were amended to require it - A.1083, A.1084 and A.1085(28); MSC.366, 373, 374 and 375(93); MEPC.246 and 247(66). Objective, paragraph 1: enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment AND assist States in implementing IMO instruments. Strategy, paragraph 3: develop an overall strategy, establish a methodology to monitor and assess it, continuously review it. Scope, paragraph 6: six subject areas - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution, STCW, load lines, tonnage, COLREG - and security is not among them. The instruments under which it is mandatory are listed in A.1187(33), adopted 6 December 2023, which revoked A.1157(32) one month before this sitting. KPIs, paragraphs 42 to 44: PSC detention rates, flag State inspection results, casualty statistics, communication and information processes, annual loss statistics excluding CTLs, plus ten review areas - all for the State's own self-evaluation. Parts 2, 3 and 4 all run implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review; coastal paragraph 48 gives eight services, port paragraph 56 gives three obligations, 59 no more favourable treatment, 62 PSCO independence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Code and what made it mandatory. 2 (a) The objective. 3 (a) The strategy. 4 (a) Which instruments. 5 (b) The performance indicators. 6 (c) Flag State. 7 (c) Coastal and port State.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2, 3 and 4 split limb (a), which hides three separate tasks inside six marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution contains the III Code, when was it adopted, and what did it revoke?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013. Its operative paragraph 3 revoked A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the revoked 2011 Code as current is a common and immediately visible error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the objective of the III Code in the Code's own words.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 1: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The second half - assistance - is routinely dropped, and it is half the sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What three things does paragraph 3 recommend a State do to meet the objective?
retrieval_cards.answer: Develop an overall strategy covering its flag, port and coastal responsibilities; establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy delivers effective implementation and enforcement of the relevant mandatory instruments; and continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve organizational performance and capability.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the "strategy recommended to flag state" half of limb (a), and it is a develop-monitor-review cycle.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The question asks which IMO instruments the Code covers. Why are there two answers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 6 defines the Code's scope as six SUBJECT AREAS - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution from ships, STCW, load lines, tonnage measurement and COLREG - and names no convention. Separately, the Code is made mandatory by amendments to the treaty INSTRUMENTS: SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and its Code, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Give both.
retrieval_cards.why: The highest-value distinction in the question and the likeliest place to lose marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which subject area is conspicuously absent from paragraph 6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maritime security. The resolution's preamble speaks of safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the six subject areas of the operative scope do not include security, so the ISPS Code and SOLAS chapter XI-2 sit outside the Code's stated scope.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who lists seven areas including security has not read paragraph 6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the flag State performance indicators at paragraph 43 and state their purpose.
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control detention rates; flag State inspection results; casualty statistics; communication and information processes; annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses; and such other indicators as may be appropriate. Their purpose is to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet the State's flag State obligations - it is self-evaluation, not a return to IMO.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) is four marks and this paragraph is the whole of it; the CTL exclusion proves the source was read.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two independence requirements appear in the Code. What are they and where?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 16.2 - the flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of any body issuing the certificates. Paragraph 62 - port State control officers must be free of commercial, financial and other pressure, hold no commercial interest in the port or the ships inspected, and not be employed by or work on behalf of recognized organizations or classification societies.
retrieval_cards.why: They sit in different Parts and serve different purposes, and are often merged into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the eight coastal State areas at paragraph 48, and say what kind of thing they are.
retrieval_cards.answer: Radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation. They are SERVICES to shipping, not controls over ships - which is the character of Part 3.
retrieval_cards.why: Giving the coastal State an inspection role is the standard error on this limb.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three port State obligations at paragraph 56.
retrieval_cards.answer: Provision of appropriate reception facilities, or the capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers.
retrieval_cards.why: The register of fuel oil suppliers is the one candidates forget.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Code says "should" throughout. How is it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: It was never redrafted into obligation language. Its USE was made mandatory by amendments to the conventions - A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) for Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) for SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; and MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) for MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: It explains the mismatch between the Code's wording and its legal effect, and the chain is recited in A.1187(33)'s preamble.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which obligations list is current at a January 2024 sitting, and what is notable about its final annex?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1187(33), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list, adopted 6 December 2023 - one month before the sitting - which revoked A.1157(32), the 2021 list. Its Annex 7 is headed "amendments expected to be accepted and to enter into force between 1 January 2024 and 1 July 2024", so at this sitting it is a forward-looking list of things that have not happened yet.
retrieval_cards.why: It is the cleanest illustration on the paper that adopted is not the same as in force.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What single shape do Parts 2, 3 and 4 of the Code share?
retrieval_cards.answer: Implementation, then enforcement, then evaluation and review. Each of the flag, coastal and port State parts is built on it, and paragraphs 42, 51 and 63 are the three evaluation requirements.
retrieval_cards.why: One remembered shape answers limb (c) for all three States and locates limb (b) inside it.
